🔵 Yukon River Inter-Tribal Watershed Council

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

An Indigenous-led grassroots coalition founded in 1997, uniting 70+ First Nations and Alaska Native Tribes across the Yukon River watershed. Guided by a vision to one day safely drink water directly from the river, YRITWC works through collaborative programs in water-quality monitoring, community education, stewardship, and sustainable resource governance. Their YRITWC Water Health Indicators complements scientific water quality monitoring with "cultural indicators", including elements like the taste of fish, the behavior of indicator wildlife species, and the quality of plants used for traditional medicines—dimensions of watershed health that conventional metrics might miss but reflect deep, multi-generational knowledge of the system.

Bioregional Context

The Yukon River—stretching over 3,100 km through Alaska, Yukon, and British Columbia—drains an expansive watershed of approximately 850,000 km². It holds profound ecological and cultural significance for dozens of Indigenous nations—Gwich’in, Koyukon, Yup’ik, Tlingit, among others—whose subsistence, social structures, and spiritual traditions are intertwined with its flows and salmon migrations. The watershed faces growing threats from climate change, permafrost thaw, mining runoff, pollution, and waste management challenges.

Place
Alaska Hwy, Yukon, YT, Canada

🔵 Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y)

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

The Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y) is a pioneering transboundary conservation network that unites governmental bodies, Indigenous groups, NGOs, scientists, landowners, and communities across a 2,100-mile corridor spanning five U.S. states and two Canadian provinces and territories. Launched in 1993, Y2Y's mission is to maintain ecological integrity and habitat connectivity from the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem in Montana/Wyoming to the Yukon Territory. The organization’s success is reflected in a 300% increase in protected habitat since its inception, along with new corridors and species recoveries .

Bioregional Context

The Y2Y region stretches across North America's Rocky Mountains—from Wyoming through Montana, Idaho, Washington, and Oregon, into Alberta and British Columbia, and ending in Yukon Territory. Covering over 1.3 million square kilometers, it overlays the territories of 75+ Indigenous nations and stands as the continent’s most intact mountain ecosystem. The region encompasses high-mountain forests, glacial valleys, and critical watersheds essential for species migrations and climate resilience.

Place
Bozeman, MT, United States

🔵 Wij land

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

In 2016, Wij.land started exploring how the 4 Returns can help restore ecological functions of the peat meadow landscape in the Vechtstreek. This has grown into a learning network of almost 200 cattle farmers today who are futureproofing their farm by learning how to work more and more alongside nature and in connection with the landscape. It plays a key role in connecting different stakeholders in the landscape to create natural, social, and financial value and to inspire others in joining this cause.

Bioregional Context

Typical for Holland, peat meadows are home to cows, windmills and (migrating) bird populations. However, the intensification of farming activities and systemic dewatering of peat soils are turning the Dutch western peat meadows into 'green deserts' where both nature and farm economics are under pressure.

Place
The Hague, South Holland, Netherlands

In New Zealand, the Whanganui River catchment forms the basis for both ecological governance and cultural identity for local Māori iwi (tribes). The recognition of the river as a legal person (Te Awa Tupua) in 2017 acknowledged both its ecological significance and its central place in Māori cultural identity and governance traditions.

The catchment includes rugged native forests, volcanic highlands, and remote rural communities, stretching from the central plateau near Mount Tongariro to the Tasman Sea.

🟡 Tarun Bharat Sangh

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

A community-led water conservation organization restoring India's river systems through traditional knowledge and modern watershed management. TBS has revived 14 rivers, built thousands of water harvesting structures, and established a network of water stewards combining technical expertise with cultural revival.

Bioregional Context

Rajasthan is India's largest state by area and one of its most water-scarce regions, characterized by arid and semi-arid landscapes with minimal annual rainfall (200-400mm). The region's water crisis is exacerbated by depleting groundwater tables, desertification, and increasingly unpredictable monsoon patterns due to climate change.

Place
Rajasthan, India
Tags
💧 Watershed_Repair ⛲ Water_Management 🔘 Governance_Bodies ♾️ Commons_Governance_Protocols 🎒 Learning_Programs 📣 Political_Advocacy 🔅 Traditional_Ecological_Knowledge 🪢 Network_Weaving 🛐 Cultural_and_Spiritual_Practices

Background


Rajasthan is India's largest state by area and one of its most water-scarce regions: arid and semi-arid country with typically 200–400mm of rain per year. Falling groundwater, desertification, and a more erratic monsoon deepen the crisis. Harvesting traditions that had sustained communities for generations were neglected in recent decades, contributing to farm decline and outmigration.

Historically, the Alwar region was water-rich into the early twentieth century. Communities practiced rainwater harvesting through johads—earthen check dams that hold runoff so it can soak in and recharge aquifers. By the 1980s scarcity was severe; parts of the region were “dark zones” in state irrigation records—groundwater critically low.

Land grew unsuitable for farming or herding, so many working-age men left for cities, leaving women and elders behind. Villages turned to Tarun Bharat Sangh after barren fields and collapsing livelihoods had already done deep harm.

Origins and Network


From 1985, Tarun Bharat Sangh (TBS), a Rajasthan-based NGO, focused on water conservation, beginning in Gopalpura in the Alwar area. The team stayed in the village to understand conditions. An elder described the old johad approach—still sound, but weakened by years without resources, backing, or confidence.

The first johad, chabootre wala johad, was built in 1985 to show the method still worked. When it held water and some farmers could grow bajra again, the team added mewalon ka baandh in 1986. Both structures helped refill wells, recharge groundwater, and restore fields.

Activities

🔸

Watershed Restoration and River Revival

TBS works with communities to bring back water abundance, revive river watersheds, and support sustainable development. Work includes harvesting structures across watersheds, efficient use such as drip irrigation, and water literacy for many actors. Before projects start, staff live in a village for six to twelve months to build trust, learn constraints, and co-design responses; engagement often runs ten to fifteen years per village. The core tools are johads, check dams, and percolation tanks, alongside literacy campaigns, drip systems, and sustainable farming. TBS reports 13,800 functioning rainwater harvesting systems and 13 rivers rejuvenated across India. Their work harvests 100 billion liters of rainwater annually and has converted more than 10,000 square kilometers from no-water zones into water-secure landscapes.

🔸

Cultural Revival for Ecological Kinship

TBS wove ritual and symbol into daily responsibility for ecosystems. Drawing on Raksha Bandhan, where sisters tie threads on brothers’ wrists, villagers tied threads around trees to pledge protection. After the first johad proved itself, Jal Utsav (Water Festival) in 1987 helped anchor community ownership; participants formed a village gram sabha (council) to share responsibility. From 1987, TBS supported three padyatras (campaign walks) each year, led by Gopalpura residents who chose routes, names, and how to invite other villages. Together, these practices frame restoration as cultural and relational—not only technical.

🔸

Community-Led Governance

To counter government contracts for commercial fishing that risked overuse, habitat harm, and displacement, TBS helped communities create the River Arvari Sansad (River Arvari Parliament) in 1998. The body drew gram sabhas from 72 villages along the river. With more than 140 members, the Parliament challenged those contracts through public-interest litigation until the Supreme Court canceled them—asserting community rights to water and land over company concessions. It sets rules for the river, banks, and catchment; for crops, fishing, grazing, borewells, and thirsty crops such as sugarcane—embodying local stewardship of shared resources. The twin villages of Bhaonta–Koylala, leaders in Arvari’s revival, received the first Down to Earth Joseph C. John award for an environmental community from President K.R. Narayanan on 28 March 2000. Similar models are spreading along rivers such as Chambal and Dholpur.

🔸

Water Literacy and Education

TBS ran trainings and workshops for farmers, youth, schoolchildren, and local officials—often through village heads—so communities could see how conservation linked to their own well-being and to the land’s productivity.

🔸

Water Warriors

TBS trained more than 10,000 Jal Yodhas (“Water Warriors”)—grassroots leaders, including women and youth—with technical and ecological skills to advance restoration locally. Tarun Jal Vidyapeeth offers a two-year course for water warriors and shorter courses for village institutions, NGOs, scientists, and officials. Many warriors organize through self-help groups and youth networks. By 2001–02, TBS had helped form 325 SHGs across 180 villages in Alwar and Mewat; women received training in plant-based medicine and took part in gram sabha decisions.

🔸

National and International Advocacy

In 1989, TBS and village partners discussed how mining in the Aravallis—near Sariska—was undermining johads. Dr. Singh concluded blasting had opened fractures in aquifers; communities needed relief. In 1990 TBS petitioned the Supreme Court to close those mines; in 1991 the Court ordered a stop, and in 1992 the Union Ministry of Environment and Forests restricted mining in parts of the range. To press state compliance, TBS and allies staged an 800-km march across four states. Dr. Singh walked from Himmatnagar, Gujarat, toward Delhi from 2 October 1993 for over four months. Advocacy of this kind contributed to closing some 28,000 mines by 1996. By 2001–02, TBS was contesting the 2002 National Water Policy, fearing it would deepen privatized control of water. The Rashtriya Jal Chetna Yatra crossed 320 districts in 30 states over fourteen months. That campaign helped launch Rashtriya Jal Biradari (RJB), a national forum in 2001 that ran roughly a decade—public meetings, riparian problem-solving, outreach to ministers and officials, and litigation where needed. In the 2020s, Jal Biradari linked to global drought-and-flood dialogue; the network claims more than 1,000 members and bodies such as the Indian Himalayan River Basin Council and the Indian Peninsular River Basin Council. With TBS vice chairman Professor G.D. Agarwal (environmentalist, former IIT Kanpur dean), the organization pressed for the Ganga. From 2008 his fasts—including over damming the Bhagirathi headstream—drew national attention. In February 2009, one outcome was national-river status for the Ganga and creation of the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGBRA).

Vision and Legacy


The programme still prioritizes highly marginalized communities—currently including Scheduled Tribe and Scheduled Caste villages in Rajasthan’s Karauli district—showing how traditional knowledge, community ownership, and long commitment can move landscapes from dry wells toward flowing water and from despair toward hope.

TBS describes five decades of work with Rajasthan communities as helping revive 14 rivers, raise forest cover by 30%, return about 70% of once-barren land to cultivation, and protect five rivers from encroachment—bringing water security to over one million families. With water came more food security and livelihood; agriculture and milk production rose in 100% of project areas and farmer incomes doubled in participating villages, giving young people reason to stay or return.

As Rajendra Singh and Indira Khurana write in “Rejuvenation of Rivers”: “Change is possible. Through love and respect: Love for nature and respect for communities, and then nurturing of both. Through understanding the terrain – the endless recharge possibilities that the fractured rocks offer – and then healing the environment through appropriate water conservation structures and involving the people and their contribution. Lastly, through maintaining transparency.”

🟡 Spruce Root

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Spruce Root is an Indigenous-led Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving 23 communities, building a regenerative regional economy by supporting Alaska Native and rural entrepreneurs.

Bioregional Context

Southeast Alaska is a coastal and island-rich region spanning over 500 miles from Yakutat in the north to Hydaburg in the south. This bioculturally significant area is the ancestral and present-day homeland of the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian peoples, whose governance, economies, and lifeways are deeply tied to the region's forests, salmon streams, and marine ecosystems.

Place
Juneau, AK, United States
Tags
✍🏾 Investment_Vehicles 🪢 Network_Weaving 🎒 Learning_Programs 🔀 Grants_Programs 🪴 Venture_Cultivation 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 💬 Peer_Learning

Background


Southeast Alaska is a coastal and island-rich region spanning over 500 miles from Yakutat in the north to Hydaburg in the south. This bioculturally significant area is the ancestral and present-day homeland of the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian peoples, whose governance, economies, and lifeways are deeply tied to the region's forests, salmon streams, and marine ecosystems—relationships forged over thousands of years.

The region includes part of the Tongass National Forest, the largest temperate rainforest in North America, and faces a complex legacy of colonial land policies, resource extraction, and economic displacement.

Origins and Network


In 2012, Spruce Root emerged in Juneau, Alaska, as an Indigenous-led Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) with a mission that went far beyond traditional lending. Founded with $500,000 in seed funding from Sealaska Corporation, one of the regional Alaska Native corporations created by the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Spruce Root was born from a vision of economic empowerment that honored the deep relationships between people, place, and prosperity.

That initial funding came from an unusual source: carbon credits from 176,000 acres of Tongass rainforest that Sealaska had set aside for carbon sequestration in partnership with The Nature Conservancy. After dominating the timber industry in the region until 2021, when Sealaska renounced commercial logging, this marked a profound shift—from extraction to regeneration, from short-term profit to long-term stewardship.

Today, Spruce Root serves 23 communities across Southeast Alaska, from Yakutat in the north to Hydaburg in the south.

Activities

🔸

Small Business Lending

Spruce Root's approach to economic development starts with recognition: many entrepreneurs in Southeast Alaska don't have access to affordable capital through traditional financing channels. But Spruce Root sees beyond credit scores and collateral. Their small business lending program targets entrepreneurs who may not qualify elsewhere, but who contribute to economic development and community well-being in the region. Before potential borrowers even apply for a loan, Spruce Root provides business and career coaching. And they continue supporting them after the loan is issued. The loans can fund startup capital, working capital, business expansion, and more. Between 2012 and 2022, Spruce Root deployed $1.2 million in loan capital. In 2022 alone, they issued loans to four Alaska small businesses totaling $350,000. In 2023, new loans deployed amounted to just under $900,000—a sign of growing momentum and trust.

🔸

Business Coaching & Programs

Lending is just one piece of a much larger vision. Spruce Root offers business coaching to stakeholders beyond their loan portfolio. In 2022, they provided business basics training to Tlingit and Haida citizens, and partnered with Sealaska Heritage Institute on developing a business curriculum for Alaska Native artists—recognizing that cultural expression and economic opportunity can thrive together.

🔸

Path to Prosperity

One of Spruce Root's signature programs is Path to Prosperity, a business development competition that supports local businesses with positive social, economic, and ecological impact. The program specifically promotes the regenerative use of the region's resources—businesses that see themselves as part of the ecosystem, not apart from it. In 2022, the competition attracted 23 applications from eight communities. The 12 finalists attended an in-person Business Boot Camp, receiving 26+ hours of training and technical assistance from 14 mentors. The goal is to build a network of businesses that understand their success is tied to the health of their communities and the land that sustains them.

🔸

Resilience Circles

With Jump/Scale, Spruce Root runs Alaska Native Resilience Circles—a year-long cohort for Indigenous entrepreneurs that treats business viability and personal and cultural well-being as one fabric. Strong communities need viable enterprises; sustainable enterprises need healthy people and cultures. The program strengthens Alaska Native businesses in ecosystem care, long-term economic resilience, overall wellness, and community mental health. Cohorts meet in person and online for workshops on personal and business finance, marketing and branding, physical health and nutrition, mental health, and Indigenous culture and values. Financial skills sit alongside cultural grounding and wellness practice. By year’s end, participants leave with sharper business tools and a denser peer network among Indigenous entrepreneurs. Spruce Root and Jump/Scale describe the work as more than training: it is part of reclaiming Indigenous knowledge, wellness, and economic sovereignty across Alaska.

🔸

Sustainable Southeast Partnership

The Sustainable Southeast Partnership (SSP)—a Spruce Root and Sealaska program—works as a regional collective-impact network. It supports collaborative, community-led responses to linked social, ecological, and economic challenges, guided by Indigenous values. Individuals, Tribal governments, Native corporations, nonprofits, agencies, businesses, and others can take part. Village-level hosts appoint community catalysts who assess energy, food, natural resources, and economic sustainability, then surface projects—from food security and energy to habitat restoration—and pair with regional catalysts on design, implementation, and tracking. Regional catalysts also shape policy, help build cooperatives and mutual support, and run workshops to grow capacity. In practice, SSP is bioregional governance: place-rooted, accountable to communities, and woven from village to region.

🔸

Strategic Planning

In 2022, they finalized and took part in implementing a five-year strategic plan for the Sitka Tribe of Alaska and began facilitating an update of the comprehensive community plan for Yakutat in partnership with the local government. These are practical tools for communities to articulate their own visions and chart their own paths forward.

🔸

Seacoast Trust

Recognizing that the work of regeneration requires long-term, patient capital, Spruce Root became the fiscal sponsor of the Seacoast Trust—a permanent funding mechanism created to provide access to capital for Indigenous-led conservation projects that place local communities at the center of efforts to achieve a healthy environment. The Seacoast Trust's guiding principles include respecting community voices, upholding Indigenous governance and leadership, and valuing the integrity of all knowledge systems—including those anchored in 10,000 plus years of Indigenous history, traditions, and stewardship. The Trust will fund the work of the Sustainable Southeast Partnership. Projects slated for funding include Native forest partnerships, healthy salmon habitat, Indigenous Guardians programs, youth leadership opportunities, food sovereignty, climate migration, regenerative economies, and reduced carbon footprints. The Trust provides grants for work programs, loans for small Tribal businesses, Southeast Tribal Land Purchases, and local infrastructure projects, as well as exchange-traded and impact funds, network coordination and capacity building. In 2022, the Seacoast Trust reached an initial $20 million funding goal with the help of Sealaska, The Nature Conservancy, and the Rasmuson, Hewlett, Edgerton, Chorus, and Wilburforce foundations. But the real vision is much larger: the goal of the trust is to reach $100 million in order to fully fund the work of Sustainable Southeast Partnership in perpetuity—ensuring that this work doesn't depend on the vagaries of grant cycles, but can continue for generations.

Vision and Legacy

What Spruce Root has built over more than a decade is something rare: a financial institution that sees its role not just as providing capital, but as cultivating economic sovereignty rooted in place and culture. They've created pathways for Indigenous entrepreneurs to build businesses that honor their values, strengthen their communities, and ensure long-term resilience.

Their work recognizes that in Southeast Alaska—a region with a complex legacy of colonial land policies, resource extraction, and economic displacement—economic development must be regenerative, not extractive. It must honor the 10,000-plus years of Indigenous history, traditions, and stewardship. It must build businesses that strengthen communities, not businesses that extract wealth and leave.

From the $900,000 in loans deployed in 2023 to the 23 communities served across 500 miles, from the Resilience Circles supporting entrepreneurs' well-being to the Seacoast Trust's vision of $100 million in permanent funding—Spruce Root is demonstrating what bioregional finance can look like when it's Indigenous-led, place-rooted, and values-aligned.

They're showing that economic development doesn't have to mean choosing between prosperity and place, between profit and principles. In Southeast Alaska, they're building an economy where businesses succeed by strengthening communities, where financial success is measured by the health of the land and the well-being of the people who call it home.

🟡 South Asia Bioregionalism Working Group

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

The South Asia Bioregionalism Working Group is a voluntary network reimagining ecoregional and bioregional governance for South Asia, challenging rigid nation-state boundaries through biocultural perspectives.

Bioregional Context

South Asia faces multiple intersecting crises—climate chaos, rising nationalism, border conflicts, and ecological degradation. The region's watersheds, like the Ganges, flow through multiple countries, divided by arbitrary borders that fragment ecological and cultural flows.

Place
India
Network Affiliation
🟣 r3.0
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 🏔️ Geographic_and_Ecological_Mapping 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 💬 Peer_Learning 🎒 Learning_Programs 🍥 Governance_Design

Background


Across South Asia, climate disruption, nationalism, border conflict, and ecological decline overlap. At the same time, thousands of grassroots initiatives are working for change.

A political map fractures the subcontinent into seven or eight countries—lines drawn by empire and colonial history. The same territory read through watersheds and culture looks different: the Ganges crosses three or four countries, its basin sliced by borders. An upstream state can dam a river with little regard for people, wildlife, or ecology downstream.

Origins and Network


In October 2019, at a Democracy Vikalp Sangam—an Alternatives Confluence in India—participants already gathered to talk about democracy asked why South Asia could not host a bioregional process of its own.

The South Asia Bioregionalism Working Group formed from that question. COVID-19 soon blocked in-person meetings, but work continued online: people kept meeting digitally to reimagine South Asia from biocultural starting points and to question nation-state lines that split ecological flows, cultural exchange, and long-standing economic ties.

The group pursues several aims. One is co-creating knowledge and awareness—advanced partly through reports now feeding modest advocacy. A larger unfinished task is helping communities on the ground reimagine their ecoregions and bioregions and, from there, influencing governance.

Activities

🔸

Learning from Practical Experiments

Before leaning on abstract theory, they looked at what was already happening. One touchstone was a river parliament catalyzed by [[Tarun Bharat Sangh]], where roughly 60 to 70 villages in one river basin in Western India built institutions to govern the basin together. They also reviewed river-basin authorities and transboundary schemes—often top-down, bureaucratic, and narrow in how they defined a river’s social and ecological life. To widen the lens, they organized about 15 webinars: practitioners described experiments on the ground; others shared bioregional work from outside the region and took part in mutual learning.

🔸

Bioregional Mapping of India

A major project set out to map bioregional boundaries across India. The team worked back from district lines imposed under British rule, layering other evidence. Sources included mythology and folklore, travelogues and explorers’ accounts, memoirs by rulers and poets, geographic writing from inside and outside the subcontinent—including colonial records—and state tourism and culture material that preserved regional names and ways of life. Through that work they mapped roughly 65 to 70 percent of India—a baseline for discussing the country’s bioregional structure.

🔸

Vision for 2100

The working group is drafting a long-range biocultural vision: what South Asia might become by 2100. In that speculative picture, borders grow permeable; visas fade. Wildlife, nomadic pastoralists, and others move more freely. Older trade corridors such as the Silk Road reappear in new form. Border zones, once flashpoints, become peace sanctuaries run locally through strong direct democracy. Today’s hyper-nationalism gives way, in the vision, to civilizational and Indigenous identities; direct democracy is rooted in villages and neighborhoods and scales up across landscapes into bioregional governance. Traders and nomadic communities act as connectors—carrying news and goods across the bioregion.

Vision and Legacy


The South Asia Bioregionalism Working Group represents a growing movement of people across South Asia who believe that reimagining governance from a biocultural perspective isn't just an interesting idea—it's essential for survival in a climate-changed world where rigid political boundaries will only create more conflict and suffering.

They've produced three reports on reimagining South Asia from a bioregional perspective, with another one or two coming out. They've organized webinars learning from bioregional approaches across the world. They're hosting a training course—a certificate course on bioregionalism with about 25 participants, put together by their collaborator ATREE with the bioregionalism working group and some of their other organizations.

They're asking fundamental questions: What if governance matched ecological boundaries? What if cultural flows weren't severed by political lines? What if the people who have lived in these bioregions for centuries could once again move, trade, and care for these landscapes as they did before colonization divided them?

The answers to these questions are still emerging. But in the work of people like Ashish, Nisha, Sonam, and Utham—in their mapping, their research, their visioning, their patient building of relationships across borders—we can see the seeds of a different future taking root.

🟡 Sinal do Vale

Bioregional Organizer

Background


Guanabara Bay is one of Brasil's largest and most iconic coastal ecosystems, framed by the Atlantic Forest and surrounded by one of the world's most densely populated urban areas. Once rich in biodiversity and cultural significance, the bay now faces severe pollution from untreated sewage, industrial waste, and urban runoff.

For over 15 years, Sinal do Vale has earned the trust and reputation in this bioregion—situated in the buffer zone between Rio de Janeiro and the Mata Atlântica rainforest. The beautiful Mata Atlântica has incredible biodiversity, but has already lost 88% of its size to date. This bioregion delivers the water, food, and other ecosystem services for Rio and surrounding areas, yet it faces urban encroachment, loss of rivers, and low economic activity leading to poverty.

Origins and Network


Against that backdrop, Sinal do Vale set out years ago to show how a biohub can act as a catalyst inside a bioregion and help grow a bioeconomy.

After 15 years of strong results on very limited budgets, the organization is now working toward self-sufficiency so it can sustain and expand that work for the bioregion.

Activities

🔸

Biocultural Hub

The site functions as a bioregional hub: a place where visitors, partners, and local actors meet, learn, and test ideas. It has developed into an internationally renowned UN Flagship Biohub—combining learning journeys, hospitality, and living prototypes of bioeconomic enterprise so regeneration is visible and repeatable, not only discussed. Two lines of work help keep the hub viable: Sinal do Vale’s own hospitality offer and the Madre Frutas social enterprise (below), which together connect revenue, training, and on-the-ground demonstration.

🔸

Madre Frutas Social Enterprise

Madre Frutas is a women-led enterprise that turns abundant local jackfruit into marketable products. It models agro-processing tied to regenerative practice, women’s leadership, and economic resilience—creating livelihoods where options are scarce while respecting what the land already provides.

🔸

Camino do Guaraú Eco-Tourism Trail

The 110-kilometer trail starts not by coincidence at Sinal do Vale. By curating this officially recognized Camino do Guaraú, Sinal do Vale galvanized entrepreneurs, activists, change makers, and farmers to join the regeneration movement. The trail reconnects the local community to its heritage, culture, and ecotourism potential. The trail continues through nine other segments in the beautiful mountain range of the Mata Atlântica. In each segment, Sinal do Vale has identified areas that need reforestation or conservation to create an agroecological belt to preserve and regenerate the biodiversity in the region. Not least among the species they're working to protect: the golden lion tamarin monkeys, an endangered species that depends on the health of this ecosystem. This work is about creating connected corridors of life, ensuring that the fragments of the Mata Atlântica can support the full diversity of life they once sustained.

🔸

Val Estrela Historic and Cultural Ecotourism Site

After about 20 kilometers through great landscapes, the trail arrives at Val Estrela—the port where one-third of the slaves arrived in Brazil. This is a site of profound historical and cultural significance, and Sinal do Vale has started executing a master plan to regenerate the rivers, the old church, and weighing station to create a historic and cultural ecotourism site. They're doing this work together with the local quilombola communities and fishermen who maintained this abandoned site over the past decades. These are communities with deep ancestral connections to this place, who have been stewarding it even as it was neglected by broader society. Sinal do Vale is determined to continue this work, recognizing that restoration must honor both the ecological and cultural heritage of this place.

🔸

Terra Umida Agroforestry Corridor

Another 30 kilometers along the trail, hikers pass wide degraded farmlands called Terra Umida. This is a government-supported area where the landless farmer movement of Brazil is working under very tough conditions to regenerate degraded land through agroforestry. Sinal do Vale has started building new supply chains for the farmer and food sector, seeing the potential to build a true bioeconomy with these farmers to benefit their livelihoods. This is about rebuilding food systems, forming regenerative supply chains with local producers, and creating economic pathways that align with ecological restoration.

🔸

SINAL Flow Fund

The SINAL Flow Fund is a locally managed funding mechanism designed to channel diverse capital streams—including public grants, donations, supply chain finance, and investment capital—toward regenerative initiatives in the region. The Flow Fund enables implementation of community-led projects by lowering access barriers to funding and supporting infrastructure for scaling a bioregional economy.

Vision and Legacy


What Sinal do Vale demonstrates is how a biohub can be a catalyst that creates the conditions for regeneration to flourish across an entire bioregion. For over 15 years, working with very limited financial resources yet achieving amazing results, they've shown what's possible when you anchor action in place, build trust with communities, and weave connections across scales from individual projects to regional bioeconomy.

From the women turning jackfruit into livelihoods at Madre Frutas to the quilombola communities restoring Val Estrela, from the landless farmers regenerating Terra Umida through agroforestry to the protection of golden lion tamarins in the Mata Atlântica—Sinal do Vale is showing how supply chains of value can regenerate landscapes that are so important for culture, for people, and for the web of life that connects us all.

🔵 Samsø Island

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Samsø is a Danish island community internationally recognized for its pioneering transition to 100% renewable energy. The community achieved energy independence through a combination of wind turbines, solar, and biomass district heating systems powered by local agricultural waste, with many installations community-owned. The island has set an ambitious target to be completely fossil fuel free by 2030, initiating conversion to electric transportation starting with the marinas.

Bioregional Context

Samsø is a small island in the Kattegat Sea between Denmark's Jutland peninsula and Zealand, with a population of around 3,600 residents. Traditionally reliant on agriculture and fishing, the island faced economic decline before reinventing itself through a community-led energy transition.

Place
Samsø, Central Denmark Region, Denmark

🟡 Salmon Nation

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

A network of public benefit companies whose purpose is to inspire, enable, and invest in regenerative development across the Salmon Nation bioregion.

Bioregional Context

The Salmon Nation bioregion spans a vast territory defined by the traditional range of wild Pacific salmon in North America, stretching from the Salinas River in California northward to the North Slopes of Alaska, unified by salmon watersheds.

Place
BC, Canada
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
💧 Watershed_Repair 🔅 Traditional_Ecological_Knowledge 🔀 Grants_Programs ✅ Result_Based_Mechanisms 🪢 Network_Weaving 🎉 Congressing_and_Events 🎨 Art_and_Storytelling ✍🏾 Investment_Vehicles 🗂️ Portfolio_Development 🪴 Venture_Cultivation

Background


For thousands of years, the salmon's annual return defined the rhythm of life for the Indigenous peoples of North America, who developed rich cultural traditions around this natural abundance. This place—where salmon and human communities have been intertwined for millennia—represents a unique bioregion now known as Salmon Nation. Today, 30 million people live within the historical range of wild Pacific salmon, citizens of this nation whether they realize it or not. They inherit the benefits of an ecosystem that, when healthy, sustains not just salmon but entire watersheds and the communities that depend on them.

The underlying principle is elegantly simple yet profound: healthy runs of wild Pacific salmon, as they journey from mountain streams to ocean and back again, connect entire watersheds and serve as a comprehensive indicator of bioregional health. When human systems—agriculture, forestry, utilities, transportation—align with natural systems, salmon flourish. And when salmon flourish, so do we.

Salmon represent what one might call a Nature State as distinct from nation-states—a place defined by natural systems that has always existed, transcending political boundaries. The salmon's return represents the greatest nutrient transfer between habitats on Earth, nourishing forests, entire food webs, and future generations. This principle has proven transformative: in the Okanagan region, a remarkable alliance including three First Nations has revitalized sockeye salmon populations from a mere 3,000 fish 25 years ago to 800,000 in 2024. These returning salmon now represent 70% of the sockeye in the once-mighty Columbia River basin, simultaneously restoring ecological function and cultural connections.

Origins and Network


The concept of Salmon Nation emerged from three decades of conservation work at Ecotrust, founded by Spencer Beebe in 1991. Through work with First Nations and rural communities across the bioregion, Ecotrust developed deep relationships and insights about bioregional systems thinking. A formative early project involved the Haisla First Nation's protection of the Kitlope River Watershed—nearly a million acres protected through the first co-management agreement in British Columbia, an experience that shaped understanding of the inseparability of ecological protection, cultural revival, and community well-being.

In 2019, this vision crystallized into Salmon Nation Trust, a public benefit LLC designed to invest in bioregional institutional infrastructure supporting regenerative development. Governed by public-benefit-oriented Trustees, the Trust channels values-aligned capital from philanthropic and mission-driven investors who do not expect financial return. The Trust serves as the foundational organization for the entire Salmon Nation ecosystem, incubating and spawning bioregional ventures while operating on the principle that healthy ecosystems and thriving communities are inseparable.

Throughout the bioregion, Salmon Nation works with what they call edge communities—smaller communities, Indigenous communities, and rural communities at the edges of modern society. In these places, they find the Ravens– smart, tough, tenacious individuals who have said, "That old industrial system doesn't work for me, and I'm going to do it differently." This philosophy recognizes that in moments of disequilibrium, it's often those at the margins who demonstrate the most innovative approaches to regenerative living.

Activities

🔸

Storytelling of Ravens

The Trust's first major initiative was Storytelling of Ravens, an in-person convening format that began in Sitka, Alaska in 2019. These gatherings brought together Ravens from across the bioregion to share personal stories of local resilience and regenerative solutions. The events emphasize emotional and relational depth, fostering transformation through shared vulnerability and celebration of what's working. From Oregon to Alaska, these annual gatherings weave together a network of changemakers who share knowledge, build relationships, and inspire collective action.

🔸

Magic Canoe

From the Storytelling of Ravens gatherings emerged Magic Canoe, a nonprofit media and storytelling organization dedicated to amplifying the people, projects, and possibilities helping Salmon Nation thrive. The Magic Canoe name comes from a story gifted by Cecil Paul, a Haisla First Nation Elder who used this story to save his home territory from logging. He described how a magic canoe grows bigger as more people join, soon holding all of us as we paddle in the same direction. As the narrative engine of the bioregion, Magic Canoe uplifts place-based innovation and regeneration through articles, videos, digital platforms, and convenings, connecting regenerative efforts across watersheds through shared visibility and values.

🔸

Edge Prize

An early experiment in funding the work of Ravens, the Edge Prize launched in 2023 as a distributed bioregional accelerator—a novel methodology for growing community through an online accelerator and prize challenge. Offering cash prizes from $500 to $20,000, the initiative convenes groups, offers learning opportunities and community building, provides funding, connects participants to additional resources, and builds a library of successful approaches. This initiative spawned [[Regenerate Cascadia]], demonstrating how small-scale catalytic funding can unlock significant community innovation when combined with learning, networking, and resource connections.

🔸

Salmon Returns

Salmon Returns is a cross-border bioregional fund grounded in the migratory pathways of wild Pacific salmon, representing what founder Cheryl Chen calls a biocultural finance collaborative for regenerating place, culture, and economy. Salmon Returns reimagines finance as an act of cultural and ecological healing, where capital returns—like the salmon—to nourish the very systems that sustain life. The fund operates through the BRIDGE Framework—a living blueprint that ensures every investment is rooted in place (Bioregional Grounding), improves biocultural function (Regenerative Design), draws from Indigenous worldviews (Indigenous Values), distributes value and governance (Distributed Ownership), circulates value rather than accumulating it (Gift Logic), and generates circular returns that sustain future projects (Enterprise Continuity). Salmon Returns supports the transition to regenerative economies by restoring biocultural landscapes, scaling community-led enterprises, and transforming finance systems. The fund has developed an emerging portfolio across the Upper Columbia River Basin and Okanagan region, the Coastal Temperate Rainforest, and the Klamath River Basin—partnering with Indigenous and local leaders to advance regenerative agriculture, watershed stewardship, and ecosystem renewal. Flagship efforts like the Okanagan Catalyst Network bring together farmers, Indigenous nations, food cooperatives, and wholesale distributors to regenerate the regional food system. The fund has mobilized over $15 million for early projects, with $15M already flowing into aligned land acquisition and distribution infrastructure. Currently raising $2M in Phase 1, with a longer-term target of $100M in catalytic capital to unlock over $1 billion in public/private investment by 2035. By 2030, the fund aims to be self-regenerating through investment returns.

🔸

Salmon Biocultural Credit Program

Salmon Returns is developing a Salmon Biocultural Credit program—a verified unit of ecological and cultural regeneration representing the restoration of salmon lifeways, habitats, and the relationships that sustain them. Unlike carbon credits that excuse harm through offsets, biocultural credits fund repair, channeling capital into living systems and turning finance from a tool of extraction into an act of reciprocity and responsibility. These credits are governed and validated by Indigenous Nations and local communities, blending traditional knowledge and science to measure real improvements in ecosystem health and cultural continuity.

Vision and Legacy


Salmon Nation is a movement built on the recognition that when salmon flourish, so do we. Through Storytelling of Ravens, Magic Canoe, Edge Prize, and Salmon Returns, Salmon Nation continues to weave together a network of changemakers, flow capital to regeneration, and demonstrate that finance can be an act of cultural and ecological healing. As the network learns to "paddle together" in the magic canoe, it offers a model for how bioregional organizations can incubate, spawn, and support regenerative transformation.

🔵 River Ericht Catchment Restoration Initiative

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Award-winning initiative bringing blended finance approaches to nature restoration, focusing on Atlantic salmon spawning grounds. Combines riparian woodland restoration, peatland protection, and habitat enhancement. Led primarily by community organizations, addressing the funding gap in nature restoration while maintaining community leadership.

Bioregional Context

Fed by upland burns from the Grampian Mountains, the catchment encompasses a mix of moorland, farmland, and wooded riverbanks. Historically important for textile milling and local agriculture, the River Ericht supports Atlantic salmon, otters, and other native species, but faces pressures from land-use change, barriers to fish migration, and climate-related flooding.

Place
Bridge of Ericht, Pitlochry, Scotland, United Kingdom

Activities

🔸

Strategy Games

From 2023-2025, a strategy game was implemented in the Ericht catchment bioregion. The process began with listening to diverse stakeholders—farmers, anglers, land managers, estate owners, and community leaders—to understand their roles and perceptions. This information formed the basis for a prototype game representing the landscape's resources and dynamics. The games help players visualize interconnections across the landscape, demonstrating how individual actions impact others' livelihoods and environmental conditions.

🔸

River Detectives

River Detectives extends the community-science approach toward catchment care. From August 2023 to August 2024, residents researched historic management of rivers, bogs, and lochans—asking what past practices might teach present stewardship. The Flax & Flood strand traced mills, weather, and water—how nineteenth-century climate shifts and extreme events shaped operations and supply. That historical ecological knowledge informs today’s questions. Part 2 turns toward systematic monitoring so communities can describe current river conditions and inform management choices.

🟡 Resilience Earth

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Resilience Earth is a nonprofit worker cooperative based in Catalonia, Spain, dedicated to transformative change through community resilience, regenerative design, democratic innovation and the social and solidarity economy.

Bioregional Context

Located in Northern Catalonia, La Garrotxa encompasses 21 municipalities with approximately 60,000 residents. It's a mountainous comarca best known for its dramatic volcanic landscape, featuring over 40 dormant volcanic cones, lush forests, and fertile valleys.

Place
Olot, Catalonia, Spain
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 🔘 Governance_Bodies 📊 Socioeconomic_Indicators 🎉 Congressing_and_Events 🎒 Learning_Programs

Background


Located in Northern Catalonia, La Garrotxa encompasses 21 municipalities with approximately 60,000 residents. It's a mountainous comarca (county) best known for its dramatic volcanic landscape. The region features over 40 dormant volcanic cones, lush forests, and fertile valleys shaped by ancient lava flows. La Garrotxa has a strong tradition of environmental stewardship, sustainable tourism, and local food systems.

Origins and Network


Resilience Earth started eight years ago when two co-founders, Erika and Oscar, began working in La Garrotxa. Today, they're a nonprofit worker cooperative of 14 people, but their approach remains fundamentally the same: working from the edge, focusing on centers rather than boundaries, building theory from practice rather than applying frameworks.

They've discovered bioregioning through doing. As Oscar reflects, "We're going really bottom up. We're not following a lot of the theoretical framework—we're kind of building one little by little as we evolve and as we work more on our territories."

Philosophy & Approach


After seven years of practice, their most useful tool became “landscape units”—a framework developed by Joan M. at the University of Girona. La Garrotxa has 2.5 landscape units, each usually spanning four to six municipalities with shared characteristics. Units can act as centers because municipalities within them are tightly interlinked. River work might span seven or eight units; ecosystem work gathers the units around a feature. The frame flexes with strategy and goal.

They focus on managing interconnectivity. From that angle, boundaries create more problems than clarity; what counts are centers—places where relationships and coherence emerge.

They set out to root change in one place—under their feet in La Garrotxa—and to convene actors around a shared aim rather than lead alone.

Activities

🔸

Beuda Democratic Innovation Project

They began seven years ago in Beuda, one of the smallest towns in La Garrotxa. Oscar says starting from the edge made sense: “It would be really difficult for us to start in the center because you know ruralities can be quite resistant to change behaviors sometimes.” Several municipalities were shifting away from long-serving “constructing mayors”—older men, often from construction—who had grown towns through housing for decades; some residents decided there were enough houses and voted differently. In Beuda they built relationships with residents pushing for change. Results have been striking: early terms brought sociocratic town elections that lasted six years and matured into circles for culture, environment, and more; government grew more open. In the latest term, the governing team stepped back; council members formed a new group and ran for office. Representatives now sit at council tables themselves—government and council partly fused. The town has inspired others. Since then, 14 of La Garrotxa’s 21 municipalities have experimented—some heavier on education, most on government, each in its own way.

🔸

La Garrotxa 2030 Strategic Planning Initiative

In late 2019, participatory governance was spreading across La Garrotxa; several rural municipalities had piloted citizen participation, often co-designed and facilitated by Resilience Earth. Seeing a chance to lift municipal learning to regional scale, they proposed co-producing a Strategic Plan for Territorial Resilience with the regional government. The president backed it politically and financially—with one condition: the plan must transform how governance is practiced region-wide. A core group of 12 people, chosen for sectoral, geographic, and cultural diversity, became the “critical yeast” tasked with keeping the process participatory and transparent enough to catalyze broader change. Months into the pandemic, they ran 17 online thematic round tables aligned with the SDGs. Over 600 people joined during COVID—“that was nuts,” Oscar recalls. To reach youth and diverse communities, they produced materials for 57 schools and held sessions in community centers and places of worship with minority groups. A wide survey drew more than 2,200 responses. In all, 40-plus participatory sessions fed a ten-year regional plan. Direct participation reached 7,000–7,500 people—over 11% of the population. They adapted the SDGs into 21 local targets (“Garrotxa SDGs”) that different actors could own, paired with an observatory of 400-plus indicators to track the plan. A tension surfaced: once strategy, indicators, and distributed governance are in place, traditional electoral politics can feel redundant. Oscar asks what remains for a party platform when “everything is been decided”—whether officials become “public service servers” carrying out what communities already decide in everyday hubs. Some elected leaders resisted, sensing the process could sideline them. They used an iceberg model to push strategies to real depth—and that resistance is still in play.

🔸

Democracy Festival (Festival Iltir)

To channel energy around that tension, they launched a Democracy Festival (Festival Iltir)—a space to surface what was moving. Interest ran high across sectors: large firms, public agencies, even the regional police chief engaged seriously. Last year’s festival drew 300 participants, including people from Barcelona and Catalonia’s national government, exploring how such processes could scale.

🔸

Local Government Incubator (INCAT)

Last year they opened an incubator for local governments—after many incubators for co-ops and nonprofits. Seven municipalities joined, all led by women—some in government, some in opposition—united in wanting a paradigm shift. Seven of twenty-one is a notable push; INCAT projects were striking in scope.

Vision and Legacy


Resilience Earth brings more than eight years of practice and a theoretical model refined in use. Two years ago the Barcelona provincial government asked them to define territorial resilience; they used the commission to consolidate learnings into a framework that continues to guide the work.

Their through-line is resilience thinking, interconnectivity, and centers over boundaries. They have shown democracy shifting in small towns, strategy emerging from broad participation, and—when governance is truly shared—politics edging toward service rather than capture.

Their experience suggests bioregional governance can change how people relate to place, how decisions are made, and how communities coordinate from the smallest municipality to the full bioregion—democracy practiced by the people who live there.

🟡 Regenerate Cascadia

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Regenerate Cascadia implements a carefully structured approach that flows from bioregion to watershed to ecoregion to local landscape, integrating indigenous knowledge and stewardship practices across the Cascadia bioregion.

Bioregional Context

Cascadia spans from Southeast Alaska to Cape Mendocino in California, extending east to the Yellowstone Caldera. Defined by the watersheds of the Fraser and Columbia Rivers, it includes 15 major watersheds and 75 distinct ecoregions, with 80% of its 18 million population living on just 12% of the land area.

Place
Cascadia, OR, United States
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 🏔️ Geographic_and_Ecological_Mapping 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 🎒 Learning_Programs 🖼️ Cultural_Hub_or_Learning_Center 🔀 Grants_Programs 🎉 Congressing_and_Events 🔘 Governance_Bodies ✍🏾 Investment_Vehicles

Background


The Cascadia bioregion stretches roughly 2,500 miles from Southeast Alaska to Cape Mendocino, California, reaching east to the Yellowstone Caldera. The Fraser and Columbia watersheds frame 15 major watersheds and 75 ecoregions. The Cascadia subduction zone has shaped this landscape for millennia—home to more than a thousand generations who have lived bioregionally, with Indigenous peoples stewarding the land since time immemorial.

Today 18 million people live here; 80% occupy about 12% of the land, mostly along the Seattle–Portland–Vancouver corridor. That concentration forms a “thin green line” with outsized influence—between interior extractive economies and markets across the Pacific.

Origins and Network


Brandon Letsinger’s path with Cascadia began in 2005. He founded the Department of Bioregion, a Seattle-based 501(c)(3) with a mission of “a world of interconnected bioregions and bioregional movements.”

At the first Salmon Nation Edge Prize in 2023, he met Claire Atwell—community artist, weaver, and organizer in Victoria, British Columbia. Together they asked how to regenerate a whole watershed, ecoregion, and bioregion across jurisdictional lines.

Regenerate Cascadia runs as a program inside the Department of Bioregion and is growing a charitable society in British Columbia to support cross-border organizing.

Their guiding question is practical and sharp: If $100 million reached their landscapes tomorrow, would they be ready to receive it? Would it reach the communities and ecosystems doing regenerative work, on their own terms? So far, the answer has largely been no.

They work through nested frames—bioregion → watershed → ecoregion → landscape. Brandon describes watersheds and ecoregions as rooms in a house: the bioregion is the house; ecoregions are not the whole system alone. Landscapes within watersheds are where people step outside and connect. The aim is to link action across scales so people see work happening, learn from neighbors, and build coherence within and between places.

Activities

🔸

Regional Activation Tour

To learn what regeneration would take, Brandon and Claire ran a month-long Regional Activation Tour in October 2023, soon after they met. With more than 100 organizers and projects around the Salish Sea and Willamette Valley, they visited 14 communities in 30 days and met over 1,000 people through talks, field visits, workshops, and interviews—all asking what it would take to regenerate an entire bioregion. Elders at each stop shared knowledge; the team documented bioregional learning around that question. They followed with an online capstone so participants could workshop and share expertise, then a Cascadia Summit to shape what Regenerate Cascadia would become. A major output was a movement map—who and what sit where, and where trust must be built through relationships, not anonymous institutions. Several core design challenges emerged. Work happens in landscapes but stays disconnected. Capacity to support it is thin. In Seattle, Brandon notes, people can discuss raising $54 billion for a third phase of light rail or hundreds of millions for schools via levies—but regenerating a watershed is often “give to your local nonprofit.” The design problem: help practitioners see their work, connect with others, and get resourced. Funding pathways for watershed regeneration are weak. Practitioners are underfunded and lack time to hunt for grants. Work stays siloed, competitive, and project-sized rather than coordinated at landscape or bioregional scale—even when funders exist, bridges to people on the ground are missing. Roughly 130–140 people stayed engaged after the tour; the movement map continues to show where regeneration lives and where new links are needed.

🔸

Hubs and Guilds Development Program

This is a structured capacity system—nested support from local landscapes to the full bioregion. It sets up landscape hubs that convene diverse actors—land trusts, solar installers, housing developers—to shape shared landscape visions with real budgets. Hubs cover defined areas and help administer bioregional regeneration funds. Guilds—communities of practice on topics landscape leaders need—produce classes, resources, and directories. An ambassador network orients newcomers to Cascadia, bioregionalism, mapping, and why those frames matter.

🔸

Cascadia Bioregion Program

BioRegen (the Cascadia Bioregion Program) tackles the “readiness” question: preparing local landscapes to absorb regenerative investment through community-led capacity. The program guides 10+ landscapes through a 12-month arc—ecological mapping, regenerative portfolios, budgeting, and success measures grounded in local priorities rather than outside corporate or government defaults. Communities self-organize into hubs that can receive and steward capital while deepening planning and governance. Work is anchored in a shared bioregional identity, living-systems principles, and long-term, trust-based investment readiness. Cohorts map assets, build portfolios, set budgets and strategies, and seed projects for funding. The BioRegen pilot (including what was called the Landscape Hub Cultivator) is underway as of 2026. It supports up to 10 Regenerate Cascadia landscape groups in an online community of practice to define what a landscape hub is and lay its foundations—interrupting entrenched patterns, treating relationship networks as essential for trust, practicing participatory governance across nested scales, and building bioregional infrastructure so funding can flow where Cascadia needs it. The first half-year emphasizes place-based regeneration strategies—bioregional mapping, nested scales of place, layers of stewardship—and a portfolio of regenerative projects per landscape with budget and story materials for communities and funders. The second half focuses on core teams, fundraising, governance, consent, carrying capacity, context-based indicators, and local funding ecosystems. Each landscape group receives $8,000 in direct support through the pilot (about $5,000 for planning and mapping and $3,000 for a flow-funding sandbox).

🔸

Cascadia Regeneration Fund

The Cascadia Regeneration Fund (“Cascade”) is Regenerate Cascadia’s vision for a living financial architecture for bioregional transition. Cities can raise billions for transit or schools; comparable mechanisms for watershed regeneration barely exist. The fund is structured as a bioregional trust, with nonprofit standing in the U.S. and Canada. The main vehicle combines three back-end donor-advised funds (DAFs) into one flow fund feeding localized landscape sub-funds, governed and regranted by hubs developed through the Bioregion Program. Governance stays as local as possible; funding reflects ongoing evaluation from communities doing the work. The intent is to let money flow like water through a coherent strategy, with metrics defined on the ground. Seeding has reached $40,000 toward an initial $100,000 goal by December 2025 to test regranting—setting up larger flows from 2026.

Vision and Legacy


They are forming an investor design circle and a funder community of practice from the recent Bioregion Conference and preparing collaborative financing forums for mid-2026. The aim is federated grant processes—coalitions around shared landscape visions—rather than isolated, project-by-project competition.

Regenerate Cascadia’s story is still unfolding: nested mapping from bioregion to doorstep, hubs and guilds that hold knowledge and money closer to place, and a regeneration fund meant to behave like the watersheds it serves. The open question remains whether Cascadia can organize quickly enough—in governance, relationships, and finance—for major investment to land where ecological and community work actually happens.

🟡 Regen Sydney

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Regen Sydney is taking a systemic view to help transition Sydney as a city and bioregion toward a life-affirming economy, moving from anthropocentrism to ecocentrism through neighborhood-scale programs and regenerative action.

Bioregional Context

Regen Sydney operates in the Sydney Basin Bioregion, on the lands of the Gadigal people. Sydney is a metropolitan city facing challenges of transgressing biophysical boundaries while not meeting social thresholds, needing to move into the safe space of the doughnut.

Place
Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia
Network Affiliation
🟣 r3.0
Tags
🍩 Doughnut_Assessment 🪢 Network_Weaving 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 📊 Socioeconomic_Indicators 📣 Political_Advocacy

Background


Regen Sydney works in the Sydney Basin Bioregion on the lands of the Gadigal people. Like many wealthy cities, Sydney overshoots ecological limits while still falling short on social foundations—the “doughnut” gap between planetary boundaries and fair social outcomes.

The bioregion mixes neighborhoods, catchments such as the Cooks River, and the wider metro area. Regen Sydney treats bioregions as open and changing—especially under climate stress—and edges between bioregions as seams of connection, not walls. Everyday rhythms—tides, seasonal bird movements, trees turning—offer handles for reconnection at neighborhood scale.

Origins and Network


Regen Sydney takes a systemic view: help shift toward a life-affirming economy by linking people already pursuing that shift, and—across generations—move Sydney as city and bioregion into the doughnut’s safe space.

It acts mainly as convenor: creating conditions for those conversations and engagements. The neighborhood scale matters because people can feel community and living systems there in concrete ways.

Activities

🔸

Sydney Doughnut Economy

They use the doughnut model with eyes open to both its strengths and limits. Adapted to Sydney, it captures place-specific ecological and social dimensions. For them it works as bridge and compass—supporting systems thinking that turns into action, speaking enough of the language of current institutions while holding a relational ethos. Across activities, it functions as a shared tool to grow systemic leadership and see past silos.

🔸

Waverley Community of Practice

In Waverley they are midway through a three-phase program. Phase one—community of practice. They invited groups already active locally—Transition Bondi, Bondi Innovation, beach cleanups, and others—and asked what regeneration in this neighborhood could mean. Over four months they balanced rigor (so institutions would take outcomes seriously) with convivial process—picnics, film nights, and similar gatherings. A community of practice of about 160 people formed; visioning held social and ecological dimensions together. Mapping exercises helped people attune to the place’s particular rhythms. Phase two—cornerstone indicators. Guided by Katherine Trebeck, they use “cornerstone” measures as a counterpoint to indicators that read as technical or illegible to the public. The idea: a small set of metrics the public can stand behind—living at the interface between institutions and communities. Cornerstone indicators braid social and ecological dimensions. One example: families who are glad not to need a car in a given area—touching transport, services, autonomy, and emissions in one indicator. Midway through phase two, they compare the neighborhood vision (informed by memory of pre-colonial conditions and honest about structural barriers) with what council is already doing, surface gaps, and ask how to measure progress toward the vision. Phase three—transition pathways. They will help people find roles in the transition. With vision and indicator-backed targets, the question becomes how the community can act together in ways that complement council and raise ambition. Methods will include live modeling games and “warm data” sessions to weave diverse knowledges. Participants have already offered sharp reflections—for instance, that connection to place can rest in a deeper spiritual bond with nature. There is no single fix; some see Waverley’s doughnut work as carrying wider significance.

🔸

Regenerative Action in Thematic Areas

A middle layer focuses on thematic work across the Sydney bioregion and metro—food systems, river restoration, and related themes. Specialists have labored in these areas for decades but are not always woven into one strategy. Regen Sydney aims to convene unlikely alliances, align intentions, and apply upward pressure on existing government layers. They are beginning with the Cooks River Alliance in a southwest catchment and are watching where that collaboration leads.

🔸

Deep Economic Code Work

The deepest layer addresses the “economic code” of the place—alliances among academia, institutions, and government to move beyond GDP toward more holistic metrics that shape decisions and finance. The tension is to pair a bold horizon with practical next steps.

Vision and Legacy


Regen Sydney works across three layers—neighborhood programs, thematic regenerative action, and deep economic code—toward civic infrastructure of interdependence.

The shift they seek is from passive consumption to active citizenship: not a vote every few years but ongoing responsibility as custodians of place and community. Through that work they hope to surface agency, connect allies, grow a movement, and clarify complementary roles.

The through-line remains: transition toward a life-affirming economy, linking people already on that path, and—over generations—moving Sydney as city and bioregion into the doughnut’s safe space, meeting social needs without breaching ecological limits.

Built on the Cosmos blockchain, Regen Network supports transparent and science-based methodologies for tracking ecological health, allowing farmers, land stewards, and communities to receive compensation for verified ecosystem services.

🟣 Regen Foundation

Support Provider
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Regen Foundation is a nonprofit organization that supports the governance, equity, and cultural integrity of regenerative finance and ecological stewardship networks. It facilitates participatory research, funding, and capacity-building for bioregional groups, while stewarding commons-based structures that bridge blockchain innovation with community-led environmental restoration.

Activities

🔸

Biocultural Jaguar Credits Program

This pilot conservation program aims to create and demonstrate a fully transparent ecological-economic model that safeguards Earth's biosphere while enhancing human wellbeing. Launched in partnership with the Sharamentsa Achuar community, the program integrates indigenous stewardship with modern technology to protect jaguar habitats. Jaguars serve as an "umbrella species"—their protection indirectly protects other species in the habitat—and are classified as endangered. The program targets 10,000 hectares of critical jaguar habitat in intact Ecuadorian jungle through blockchain-verified conservation credits. A robust monitoring and reporting plan, including satellite, cameras and community monitoring, supports validation of credit issuance. The credits are based on the peer-reviewed ERA Biodiversity Stewardship Methodology and issued on the open Regen Network Registry. By the time of its launch in 2024, the program had already secured $75,000+ in pre-sale commitments, representing two-thirds of initial credit availability.

🟡 Reconnecting Northland

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Reconnecting Northland supports socio-ecological transformation and community-led regeneration across Northland, New Zealand. It empowers communities through long-term partnerships and localized projects that enhance biodiversity and resilience. They are working across approximately 150,000 hectares of forest, watersheds, rivers, wetlands and farmlands in Northland, with a goal of 800,000 hectares by 2050.

Bioregional Context

Northland (Te Tai Tokerau) forms the narrow peninsula at the northern tip of New Zealand's North Island, surrounded by the Pacific Ocean and Tasman Sea. The region features diverse ecosystems including coastal wetlands, kauri forests, and dune lakes, but has experienced significant habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss through colonial-era deforestation and agricultural conversion. Despite ecological degradation, Northland retains the highest biodiversity in New Zealand and has the country's highest proportion of Māori population.

Place
Northland, New Zealand
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 🏵️ Habitat_Connectivity 📚 Training_and_Employment_Pathways ⛓️ Value_Chain_Development 🪴 Venture_Cultivation 🔀 Grants_Programs ✍🏾 Investment_Vehicles 🔅 Traditional_Ecological_Knowledge 💧 Watershed_Repair

Background

Northland (Te Tai Tokerau) holds Aotearoa New Zealand’s highest native biodiversity, yet decline continues: underfunded volunteer efforts, especially in low-income communities, cannot match the pace of loss. Short, steep rivers could recover quickly if sediment and habitat stress were addressed systemically, but catchments remain degraded.

A large Māori population carries deep whakapapa to whenua—both a demand for justice in resource decisions and a reservoir of kaitiakitanga for regeneration.

Climate shocks and eroding ecosystems now answer decades of underinvestment in care. Central agencies work in silos; electoral cycles chop programmes before they root. Communities often see what is needed yet lack capital, coordination, and time to sustain action.

Origins and Network


Whenua ora, waiora, tangata ora — Land, Water, and People Flourishing Together for the Northland Bioregion of Aotearoa.

This is Reconnecting Northland's vision: a future where thriving ecosystems are the cornerstone of sustainable communities and regenerative local economies. As a Connectivity Catalyst, Reconnecting Northland inspires the connections and weaves the relationships required for community-led socio-ecological regeneration to occur across large landscapes.

They imagine how community environmental efforts can evolve into innovative, connected, resilient, and financially sustainable ventures—capable of working together to heal the social and environmental fragmentation inhibiting Northland's prosperity.

The movement toward sustainable communities follows a structured, phased approach.
1. In Phase 1, they facilitate community visioning and planning by supporting intergenerational dialogue and advising on the Connectivity Action Plan (CAP) process, while helping establish local governance structures.
2. Phase 2 focuses on resourcing and supporting community needs by applying Te Kete Hononga to address training, service access, and capacity building, ultimately growing local capability.
3. In Phase 3, they align funding and investment opportunities with the CAP and foster investment partnerships for local nature-based enterprises.
4. Phase 4 involves the implementation of landscape-scale initiatives, along with monitoring and reporting their impacts.
5. Finally, in Phase 5, they support the development of local regenerative economies, with nature-based enterprises underpinning sustainable community growth.

Activities

🔸

Te Kawa Waiora

In 2020–2021, Te Kawa Waiora examined mauri—life force—along the Wairoa River and its margins, centring Indigenous partners and asking what a renewed, place-based ethics of care might look like. Findings pointed to a “new sacred”: honouring tūpuna insight while meeting present and future pressures. Lasting river health, the work argues, needs shared responsibility across hapū and towns. Co-designed with mana whenua, wānanga brought leaders and knowledge holders together. Outputs include a living framework for decisions that protect ecosystem mauri, intergenerational wellbeing, and relational duty. Te Kawa Waiora still orients regeneration efforts across the region.

🔸

Tapere: Planning Rooted in Ancestral Boundaries

Tapere builds hyper-local plans aligned with Māori tapere land units—not imported grid lines. Reconnecting Northland supports hapū and whānau to state restoration goals that match culture and geography. Wānanga, story, and mapping invite communities to picture thriving ancestral estates. Visions then steer practical work—planting, stream repair, nature-based enterprise—through a shared cultural lens, with connectivity and corridors treated as landscape-scale outcomes.

🔸

He Ripo Kau: A Vision for the Hokianga

He Ripo Kau applies the Tapere logic in Hokianga—linking taiao renewal with mana tangata. Since 2016, hui have convened hau kāinga around a shared model. NZD 3.2 million in Provincial Growth Fund support underpinned a 2020 recovery and employment wave—45+ km of stream fencing, 50+ ha planted, and training pipelines into land-care jobs. The case shows vision translating into paid, on-ground regeneration.

🔸

Te Kete Hononga: The Basket of Connections

Te Kete Hononga (“basket of connections”) bundles navigation support for community initiatives: funding, training, and agencies threaded through a trusted Kairaranga (weaver)—a local person trained to open doors across the system. One contact per community reduces friction with fragmented government programmes while keeping authority close to whānau knowledge and aspirations.

🔸

Nature-Based Enterprise

Nature-based enterprise ties livelihoods to healthy ecosystems inside each Tapere. Deprivation—scarce jobs, housing stress, thin services—slows circular economies even where biodiversity is high. Reconnecting Northland co-designs ventures that convert cultural and ecological capital into revenue, then helps align investment and fair flows so income supports regeneration rather than extracting from it.

🔸

The Connectivity Partnership

The Connectivity Partnership formalises cooperation among NGOs (WWF-New Zealand, NZ Landcare Trust), agencies, and iwi—pooling knowledge, co-funding, and coordinating corridors and catchments. It helped lift neighbourhood projects toward landscape strategies for biodiversity, pests, and water that braid western science with Māori worldviews. A parallel aim is syndicated investment: government, philanthropy, and impact capital opening shared windows for community priorities.

Vision and Legacy

Decades of conservation spending have not reversed trendlines; Reconnecting Northland argues for intervening in systems—behaviour, finance, governance—not only isolated projects.

The group works at landscape scale—today roughly 150,000 ha, toward 800,000 ha by 2050—so whenua, wai, and tangata can flourish together.
