🟡 Blue Ridge Foodshed Fund

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Blue Ridge Foodshed Trust emerged in the aftermath of Hurricane Helen as a response to the mounting instability of the global food system and the deep vulnerabilities of rural communities. The Trust's mission is to localize food systems by supporting small-scale farmers, building regenerative distribution infrastructure, and addressing food access through community-centered investment.

Bioregional Context

The Blue Ridge bioregion spans the ancient Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States, encompassing parts of Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee. Characterized by temperate forests, rolling hills, and biodiverse watersheds, the region has long supported resilient agricultural traditions and community-based food systems.

Place
Southern Blue, 132 W Bankhead St, New Albany, MS 38652-3313, United States
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
🍽️ Community_Food_Access 🚚 Regional_Sourcing ⛓️ Value_Chain_Development 🔀 Grants_Programs ✍🏾 Investment_Vehicles 💠 Collective_Ownership_Models 🍥 Governance_Design

Background


The Blue Ridge Mountains are among the oldest and most biodiverse landscapes on Earth—over 1.2 billion years old, older than the Atlantic Ocean. Cherokee people and their ancestors have stewarded these mountains for roughly 12,000 years. In September 2024, Hurricane Helene tore through the region and exposed a structural tension: western North Carolina still hosts more than 5,000 family farms, numerous aggregators and distributors, and 40 farmers' markets, yet only about 4% of food purchased locally is produced in the region—underscoring how fragile long supply chains are and why many residents are recommitting to bioregional food sovereignty.

Origins and Network


The Blue Ridge Foodshed Trust was formed as a nonprofit corporation with a mission to rapidly localize the regional food supply. The Trust brings funding and resources into the region through trusted relationships with mission-aligned partners. Rooted in the Western North Carolina community, the Trust serves as a valuable intermediary with deep knowledge of the foodshed's challenges, needs, and assets.

Activities

🔸

Farm Food Access Program

The Farm Food Access Program is the Trust’s lead intervention: it pays farmers for food that is then prepared or boxed for community resource centers across six counties—getting dollars onto farms while feeding neighbors through trusted front-line organizations. The design grew from an eight-week pilot backed by a $1 million American Red Cross grant. The theory of change is straightforward—pay producers first, widen the program, and over time reduce dependence on one-off disaster and charity dollars by knitting in schools, institutions, and households as reliable buyers, supported by storytelling that builds demand for local food. Operations lean on Fastroots, a platform for spotting needs, coordinating resources, tracking impact, and sharing transparent, community-held data.

🔸

WNC Food Hub Collaborative

The WNC Food Hub Collaborative is a newly formed group of 10 participating food hubs across the region that collectively purchase from hundreds of local farms. This existing network of aggregation, storage, and distribution capacity provides the foundation upon which a truly integrated regional food system can be built. The Trust works to strengthen and integrate this local food supply chain, reducing inefficiencies, building infrastructure, and expanding capacity.

🔸

Institutional and Commercial Purchasing

Schools, universities, and hospitals could anchor steady demand for regional farms, but procurement rules, food-safety expectations, and thin coordination often block uptake. The Trust is bundling responses: procurement subsidies that reimburse institutional and commercial buyers for verified local purchases; investment in aggregation and food-safety capacity so farms can meet buyers where compliance is non-negotiable; and digital links between hubs and institutions to cut administrative friction.

🔸

Blue Ridge Community Land Agreements

Recognizing that land access is a major barrier for small-scale and BIPOC farmers in the region, the Trust is developing a land strategy based on long-term stewardship rather than speculative ownership. The team is working with landowners in three target landscapes who are willing to enter into long-term agreements that prioritize food production and ecological regeneration. These regenerative land trusts will acquire and permanently protect farmland at risk of development, provide affordable land access to farmers through below-market rates, and ensure long-term affordability for local growers while scaling regional production capacity. The agreements may include community easements, stewardship covenants, or lease-to-own models that favor equity, regenerative production, and generational succession.

🔸

Blue Ridge Foodshed Capital Infrastructure

The Trust is partnering with Abundance Capital to administer the Blue Ridge Foodshed Fund—a catalytic donor-advised fund (DAF). This multi-donor fund receives tax-deductible grants from public, private, and corporate donors, creating a capital pool for grants, zero/low-interest loans, and return-based investments. Returns flow back into the Fund to be reinvested in more initiatives. The team is identifying catalytic projects in three specific landscape clusters across the region. Potential investments include local processing and aggregation centers, mobile market units, cold storage solutions, and co-located services for farmers and food entrepreneurs.

🔸

Producer-Centered Governance Design

A core tenet of the Foodshed Trust model is that producers must play a central role in funding decisions, infrastructure design, and enterprise development. The organization is hosting a series of listening sessions and design workshops with producers across the region to co-create these governance models. Over time, these governance frameworks will be embedded into the operation of the Trust's capital vehicles and community land tools.

Vision and Legacy


Localizing western North Carolina’s food system offers measurable returns in four areas: economic vitality, public health, ecological repair, and community resilience. The Trust treats those returns as mutually reinforcing—farm income, eater access, watershed health, and civic capacity rising together when capital, land, and governance align around producers.

🟡 Bioregioning Tayside

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Bioregioning Tayside takes a non-anthropocentric, place-based approach to regional regeneration, centering ecological systems alongside human communities. Guided by the principle "change the frame, change the story," the initiative aims to cultivate new narratives of place that support resilience in the face of climate disruption, biodiversity loss, and economic instability.

Bioregional Context

A substantial region in Central Scotland centered around the River Tay catchment system, extending from mountains through to the Tay estuary. The area encompasses diverse landscapes, including one of Europe's most important Atlantic salmon spawning grounds. Their bioregion represents a significant portion of central Scotland's landmass, with varied ecosystems from highland to coastal areas.

Place
Perth, Scotland, United Kingdom
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
🧪 Citizen_or_Community_Science 💧 Watershed_Repair 🌱 Vegetation_Planting 🏵️ Habitat_Connectivity 📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 🌀 Systems_and_Resource_Mapping 📋 Finance_Assesments 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Social_or_Network_Mapping

Background

Tayside is a large swath of central Scotland organized around the River Tay catchment—from mountain headwaters to the estuary—where Atlantic salmon and varied ecosystems tie upland, strath, and coast into one hydrological story. The initiative treats that whole gradient as the practical frame for regeneration work.

Origins and Network

Bioregioning Tayside grew out of the Cateran Ecomuseum’s “museum in the landscape,” which prepared the lead organizers to think at bioregional scale. They stay connected across Tayside and with peer initiatives such as [Bioregional Learning Centre South Devon]], which helped them get started. [The core team is small, held together by long collaboration, friendship, and shared care for the living world.

A theory of change and catchment-wide strategic goals are still in draft. Learning is mostly organic—convened when an issue forces collective attention—and technical support is bought in when grants allow (for example, a leading Scottish food journalist serves as Food Ambassador).

Activities

🔸

Tayside Community Science Initiative

As one of five NatureScot pilots, the initiative asks how community-led monitoring can strengthen resilience and regeneration—grounded in place-based knowledge, shared learning, and collective agency. An opening mapping phase surfaced recurring problems: incompatible methods across groups, weak hooks to regional or national strategies, and cases where communities collect extensive data but rarely see direct benefit. The team is now documenting live examples—from flood monitoring to heritage work on how Strathmore land-use history altered water paths—and asking what adaptive governance would mean for community monitoring that actually feeds decisions.

🔸

River Ericht Catchment Restoration

The Ericht is among Europe’s most important Atlantic salmon spawning systems. Restoration finance nationally falls short of need; new policy instruments are appearing, and this project is testing how to operate in that shifting policy and funding terrain. Work includes woodland and peatland restoration, with salmon survival as the narrative anchor: as one participant put it, many doubt salmon can persist—“but we’re going to do our best to see what we can do.” Habitat repair is treated as the decisive lever for keeping salmon in these rivers.

🔸

River Detectives

River Detectives extends the community-science approach toward catchment care. From August 2023 to August 2024, residents researched historic management of rivers, bogs, and lochans—asking what past practices might teach present stewardship. The Flax & Flood strand traced mills, weather, and water—how nineteenth-century climate shifts and extreme events shaped operations and supply. That historical ecological knowledge informs today’s questions. Part 2 turns toward systematic monitoring so communities can describe current river conditions and inform management choices.

🔸

Strategy Games

From 2023-2025, a strategy game was implemented in the Ericht catchment bioregion. The process began with listening to diverse stakeholders—farmers, anglers, land managers, estate owners, and community leaders—to understand their roles and perceptions. This information formed the basis for a prototype game representing the landscape's resources and dynamics. The games help players visualize interconnections across the landscape, demonstrating how individual actions impact others' livelihoods and environmental conditions.

🔸

Stocktake and Gap Analysis

Between autumn 2024 and early 2025, two directors held ten conversations with [[Dark Matter Labs]], working through fifteen dimensions of how the Tay might one day host bioregional financing facilities without being pulled into finance-as-usual.The stocktake and gap analysis summary names what followed: most effort still moves on grants; directors absorb much of the labour unpaid; the orchestrated live portfolio stays narrow while a longer shelf of ideas waits on restricted funds and courage. Relationships with power and place are understood in the room more often than in a single shared atlas; bioregion-wide visioning is deliberately cautious because neighbours want motion, not another talking shop. Pilots such as the Ericht point toward MRV and a possible nature-finance aggregation path, yet no Tay-dedicated financial vehicle exists—only the question of what must harden first so a facility could be trustworthy rather than ornamental.

Vision and Legacy

Priorities on the horizon include deeper mapping (including carbon sequestration options), a possible nature-finance aggregation platform so varied restoration projects can connect to capital, regenerative tourism, and more intentional choices about digital tools—alongside persistent questions of skills and governance. Funding remains the binding constraint: work is overwhelmingly grant-funded, nature-finance experiments are fragile under policy and corporate uncertainty, and no dedicated bioregional financial institutions exist yet. Engagement has been project-led and trust-based; a full bioregion-wide visioning process is still pending. Land and power in Scotland, thin investment in relationships, capacity gaps for restoration at pace, burnout, and the sheer complexity of restoration all slow change—yet visible projects and community voice are shifting what Tayside believes is possible, with arts and culture seen as under-used levers when resources allow.

Tags

Background

The Bride Valley, which is part of the Copper Coast UNESCO Geopark, is characterized by a primarily agricultural landscape—a mix of dairy farms, grazing lands, and areas being transformed for nature conservation. Multiple generations of family farms form the backbone of the local economy, creating a context where sustainable transitions must work with existing farming communities rather than replacing them.

Origins and Network

The Bioregional Weaving Alliance Ireland (BWA Ireland) is a bioregional initiative functioning as a transition hub, learning centre, and living lab. Established as a non-profit in 2022, the organization brings together a network of Irish stakeholders, partners, and the living systems of the region itself.

The organization is involved in a 'deep demonstration' partnership with the Irish government to test landscape approaches to the future of sustainable dairy, positioning them to establish the Bioregional Weaving Alliance as an entity designed to support learning and initiatives leading to bioregional regeneration, restoration, and protection, especially in the South East.

Activities

🔸

Family Land Biodiversity Index

A project involving 43 farmers with the goal of ensuring at least 10% of farmland is dedicated to biodiversity while maintaining farm viability. To this end, they developed the Family Land Biodiversity Index (FBI), a tool designed to reward farmers for ecological stewardship. Unlike traditional conservation schemes that rely on static subsidies for setting aside land, the FBI is a results-based incentive system with four components: biodiversity survey, farm-specific biodiversity plans, annual biodiversity scoring, and results-based payments. The project developed a digital tools to accurately measure space for nature on farms and verify the ecological quality of these areas. The outcomes of the project were exciting. Farmers reported 5–10% revenue increases through diversified income sources, such as agroforestry and eco-tourism. The 43-farm discussion group created a strong social fabric, and even neighboring farms started creating their own habitat corridors. This created biodiversity gains including pollinator population recovery, recovery of ground-nesting bird species, and improved soil health. The FBI model is now being considered for wider agricultural policy reforms at the national and EU level.

🔸

Sustainable Dairy Index

Building on the FBI system, the team developed the Sustainable Dairy Index, a systematic effort to redefine success metrics in dairy farming by integrating environmental and social returns alongside financial ones. The program introduces frameworks for measuring social contributions, recognizing that when farmers depend on other farmers, they create circular economies and sustainable economies.

🔸

Dunhill Ecopark Development Initiative

Dunhill Ecopark is a community-scale hub meant to combine living, working, learning, and enterprise: roughly 38 businesses already operate on-site, with education spaces anchoring how people encounter regenerative agriculture and reflect on environmental, social, and economic impacts together. A planned on-site milk-processing facility would keep more value from regenerative dairy in the territory—linking premium products to fair returns for farmers. The hub mixes earned income, grants, and investment so the site can stay viable while the model is tested at scale.

🔸

Regenerative Agriculture Demonstration Network

Demonstration farms knit neighboring holdings into a learning network—sharing practices and materials in place. One early experiment uses waste wool as mulch around aronia berries. The longer-term bet is that these sites become reference points: for farmers trying new crops, for visitors relearning relationships to food and land, and for shifts in what people grow, buy, and expect from the landscape.

🔸

Waterford Bioregional Mapping

Mapping work combines science and lived attachment. Participatory workshops ask residents where they feel emotionally tied to the territory; those insights layer onto geological base maps of river basins and land use. In the Anne Valley, community-led water-quality monitoring adds ground-truth to institutional data. Throughout, the process engages Gaeltacht na nDéise (Irish-speaking Waterford) so language and culture stay visible in how the bioregion is drawn and discussed.

Vision and Legacy

Through their deep demonstration partnership with the Irish government and their portfolio of initiatives, BWA Ireland is positioned to serve as a vessel for change—inspiring farmers, communities, and visitors to participate in regenerative practices that benefit nature, farmers, economy, and inspiration. The work demonstrates how locally-driven initiatives can scale up through policy influence (as with the FBI model), while maintaining strong community roots and collaboration at the bioregional level.

🟡 Bioregional Learning Centre South Devon

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

The Bioregional Learning Centre (BLC) in South Devon works at the intersection of geosystems, human systems, and ecosystems to build long-term climate resilience and civic capacity. Its work is structured around four key pillars– developing place-based funding ecosystems; enabling citizen-led data collection and analysis to track vitality and adaptive capacity; supporting community groups with evidence for effective representation in governance; and fostering systems thinking through education and cultural engagement.

Bioregional Context

The region is defined by five rivers, with the River Tamar in the west (serving as the historic 7th century Cornwall-Devon boundary) and River Tean in the east. All rivers rise from Dartmoor in the north, flowing to the English Channel in the south. They recognize potential connections to a wider "Channel bioregion," noting stronger commonalities with French coastal communities than northern neighbors. The landscape is characterized by multiple river valleys that shape both the physical environment and human settlement patterns.

Place
River Dart, Greenway Road, Brixham, TQ5 0, United Kingdom
Tags
👁️‍🗨️ Storying_Place 🍩 Doughnut_Assessment 💧 Watershed_Repair 🧪 Citizen_or_Community_Science 🦏 Rights_of_Nature 🤝🏾 Agreements_and_Legal_Instruments 🎨 Art_and_Storytelling 🧳 Immersive_Journeys 🎒 Learning_Programs

Background


The Bioregional Learning Centre (BLC) in South Devon operates in a region defined by five rivers flowing from Dartmoor in the north to the English Channel in the south. The River Tamar in the west has served as the historic boundary between Cornwall and Devon since the 7th century, while the River Teign marks the eastern boundary.

Origins & Network


The Bioregional Learning Centre prioritizes relationships in how they describe and work with bioregions—focusing on the ability to build relationships, create connective tissue, and understand natural boundaries. They work at the intersection of geosystems, human systems, and ecosystems, understanding how living systems are changing, and how to adapt.

Philosophy & Approach


The organization has identified four foundational pillars necessary to sustain their work long-term:

1. Finance: Developing place-based funding ecosystems for bioregional work.
2. Data and Metrics: Enabling citizen-led data collection, use, access, sharing, and interrogation. .
3. Governance: Supporting community groups with solid information and evidence for effective representation.
4. Arts and Culture: Using creative engagement to connect communities with place and ecological issues they cannot directly experience.

Together, these pillars form resilient infrastructure: data informs governance, which strengthens community agency, and attracts contextually appropriate funding.

Activities

🔸

Story of Place

To understand the boundaries and character of their bioregion, the BLC undertook a Story of Place process, creating a layered analysis starting from geology, examining landscape and land use, rainfall patterns and soil types, but also human social history and political history. This process sought to understand how human culture has been shaped by the natural characteristics of the region.

🔸

Devon Doughnut Project

In 2020, as the world grappled with the global pandemic, the BLC recognized an opportunity to reimagine their bioregion's future through Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics model. The BLC convene an action design collective, which grew in a year from about seven people to 170. For each domain of the doughnut economics framework, they gathered experts working on the ground in different sectors: coastal marine health, livelihood and work, political voice, and others. Participants identified leverage points in each domain, as well as pathways to action– one particular scenario in each domain that has the power to drive a significant shift. The collective also developed a framework using twinned indicators to create pathways for both citizens and policy makers working side by side. The process produced the Devon Doughnut—an interactive website capturing the current state of affairs in the region, proposing indicators and ways to track them, plus suggested actions to regenerate communities and ecosystems.

🔸

Dartington Charter & Dance

The UK's first River Charter was established at Dartington in 2019, which recognizes the river's intrinsic rights alongside its role in supporting biodiversity and community wellbeing. The Charter has since been integrated into Dartington's Neighbourhood Plan and local religious pilgrimage routes.

🔸

Dancing in Salt Marshes

The program pairs salt-marsh restoration and water conservation with cultural engagement—including work toward river rights charters—so ecology and culture move together rather than as separate “environmental” and “arts” tracks. Because the marshes are too fragile for heavy visitation, the BLC commissioned a film: two dancers from local communities perform in costume on the marsh itself, giving people a visceral connection to a place many will never walk on.

🔸

Climate Adaptation Learning Journey

Over five days, participants move through the bioregion—farms, coasts hit by flooding, river communities facing high water, sites where people are repairing roads themselves—linking water quantity and quality to everyday decisions. The aim is twofold: strengthen communities as first responders to local climate risk, and work with elected councillors so adaptation strategies are co-produced rather than imposed from outside.

Vision and Legacy


The BLC has been doing extensive projects, particularly on rivers, engaging local people in thinking about drought, water conservation, salt marsh restoration, and river charters. Increasingly, they recognize the need to put a platform or pillars underneath their work to sustain it long-term—the four pillars of finance, data and metrics, governance, and arts and culture. This approach has produced tangible outcomes—from river charter co-development and Devon Doughnut economic frameworks to regional ecosystem interventions and innovative arts-based engagement connecting communities with place.

🟡 Bay Delta Trust

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

The Bay-Delta Trust, fiscally sponsored by the Buckminster Fuller Institute, operates as a weaving and convening initiative focused on improving network coordination and increasing regenerative investments in the bioregion. Their approach builds on a rich history of bioregional work in the area, including Peter Berg's influential contributions through the Planet Drum Foundation in the 1970s, which helped establish early municipal environmental programs.

Bioregional Context

The San Francisco Bay-Delta bioregion encompasses the largest tidal estuary on the west coast of the Americas, centered around the San Francisco Bay and Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The region is defined by its watershed drainage basin, which extends well beyond the immediate bay area to include multiple counties in California. The Mediterranean climate shapes key regional concerns around water, food, and fire management.

Place
California St, San Francisco, CA, United States
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 🧳 Immersive_Journeys 🎒 Learning_Programs 🌀 Systems_and_Resource_Mapping 📣 Political_Advocacy

Background


In the San Francisco Bay–Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta bioregion, Coast Miwok and Ohlone peoples and their ancestors sustained relations with the land and water over countless generations—interwoven, like coast redwoods that support one another though their roots are shallow, so the grove stands.

More recently, Peter Berg—an early voice for bioregionalism—made San Francisco a base. In the mid-1980s he convened Bay Area groups to draft the Green City Program for urban sustainability, published in 1989, and helped organize annual Shasta Bioregion Gatherings across Northern California. Today’s initiatives draw on both Indigenous continuity and that later bioregional lineage.

Origins and Network


Lawrence Grodeska founded the Bay-Delta Trust, a weaving and convening initiative seeking to improve network coordination and increase regenerative investments in their bioregion. The organization, fiscally sponsored by the Buckminster Fuller Institute, explores new place-based models of pluralistic governance and collaboration.

Activities

🔸

Bay Delta Community Learning Ecosystem

A strategic network-building initiative that combines monthly community calls highlighting local projects with Bioregional Explorers Club field trips to build direct experience of the watershed. The program brings together diverse stakeholders through regular strategy workshops and community gatherings, focusing on building relationships and shared understanding across the bioregion.

🔸

Bay Delta Asset Mapping

The Trust leads an asset-mapping process that asks: What strengths already exist in this system—institutions, people, projects, built and natural assets—and how can they be named, mapped, and made easier for others to find and build on? Community sessions, evolving digital tools, and ongoing data collection together build a shared picture of capacity across the bioregion.

🔸

Bay Delta Governance Innovation

Governance innovation proceeds along four connected lines: partnering with aligned institutions; targeted education for agencies (including taking water-district officials on watershed tours); engaging private landowners in restoration; and experimenting with “partner state”–style arrangements that widen who stewards decisions. The work connects to existing funding streams—such as California’s nature-based solutions programs—while building skills and relationships for bioregional-scale coordination.

Vision and Legacy


The Trust describes itself as still in a discovery phase: listening, interviewing, and mapping partners with humility before large commitments. The aim is a 10,000-day horizon toward a 100-year vision for the Bay–Delta—a container where anyone can contribute how they imagine quality of life and a livable watershed.

🟡 Atelier LUMA

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Atelier LUMA operates as a biodesign lab in the Camargue region of southern France, connecting human and non-human elements through design interventions. The organization transforms undervalued local resources into valuable materials and products while maintaining a multidisciplinary team of approximately 20 people.

Bioregional Context

Located 45 kilometers from the Mediterranean Sea in southern France, the region sits between the sea and Camargue National Park. The area is characterized by its former industrial heritage, operating from a converted railway station that once housed industry.

Place
The Camargue, Lieu-dit Arnella, 13460 Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer, France
Tags
🎋 Materials_Transformation 🧦 Clothing_and_Product_Manufacturing 🏗️ Construction_and_Infrastructure 🏞️ Demonstrator_Site 🪢 Network_Weaving 💬 Peer_Learning ⛓️ Value_Chain_Development

Background


The Camargue region of southern France stretches between the Mediterranean Sea and Camargue National Park, a landscape shaped by both natural processes and industrial heritage. Atelier LUMA operates from a converted railway station in Arles, part of the Luma Arles cultural institute.

Origins and Network


Atelier LUMA functions as a biodesign lab where "bio" encompasses both human and non-human elements and how they live together. Their core principle guides their approach: materials are heavy and should stay local, while ideas and people are light and should be global. The organization emerged from Jan Boelen's work developing biolabs across Europe, including one in Ljubljana inspired by projects like the Santian Eco City Lab.

Atelier LUMA discovers undervalued resources in a region—heritage, science and technology, crafts, existing needs—and connect them through design processes. The organization maintains a multidisciplinary team of approximately 20 people—designers, biologists, engineers, and lab technicians—enabling work across disciplines from material research and development to prototyping and knowledge transmission.

Activities

🔸

Resource Transformation and Material Development

A central focus involves identifying and transforming undervalued resources into valuable products and materials. They work with Mérinos d'Arles sheep wool, exploring natural dyeing techniques and new applications that can reactivate industries and reconnect value chains while avoiding plastics. The organization examines how seeds can be made with rice—common in the Camargue—and explores the leftovers of olive pressing, extruding and mixing them with minerals to create chairs. They investigate salt—one of the most abundant materials in the world—exploring crystallization processes that only use wind and sun to produce wall applications in buildings, valuable for energy-efficient construction. Beyond material development, they create software and documentation for these age-old materials, showing how they can be used in different ways and shared with design communities.

🔸

Sustainable Building Demonstration

One of their most significant projects is the comprehensive renovation of a 2,000-square-meter industrial building on the Luma Arles site. Completed over three years in collaboration with two architectural teams, the project demonstrates sustainable construction principles. They developed 20 materials from the region within a 70-kilometer radius, using the building site itself as a key source. The building is connected by the materials with the landscape, but it's also an ecosystem in itself—collecting gray, green, and yellow water to irrigate gardens, with water filtered by algae used in their research programs.

🔸

Biofabric Places Network

The Biofabric Places Network is a collaborative system of material production hubs. The network enables different bioregions to learn from each other—materials "cooked" in similar ways but adapted to local contexts, from Middle Eastern deserts to European cities. Each time, they work together with industries, universities, and build local networks with cities and various partners to find cooperatives that can continue building and producing these materials locally. They're mainly focused on building materials, examining how waste streams in cities and larger regions can contribute to a healthier building industry.

Vision and Legacy


All this methodology is written down in their book, Atelier Luma: Bioregional Design Practices. This publication shares their approach to finding, connecting, implementing, and transmitting bioregional design knowledge with broader communities, demonstrating how locally-driven material innovations can scale while respecting bioregional specificity—enabling knowledge to flow globally while materials remain rooted in place.

🟡 Amazon Sacred Headwaters Alliance

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Established in 2017, the Amazon Sacred Headwaters Alliance unites indigenous nationalities across Ecuador and Peru to protect their ancestral territories. The alliance operates through indigenous-led governance, cross-border collaboration, integration of traditional decision-making, and strategic partnerships between indigenous communities and NGOs to safeguard one of the Amazon's most biodiverse regions.

Bioregional Context

The region encompasses 35 million hectares spanning Ecuador and Peru, where the Andes mountain range meets the Amazon basin. This creates dramatic elevation changes from 6,000 meters in the Andean glaciers to less than 500 meters in the Amazon lowlands. The area represents one of the Amazon's most biodiverse hotspots, containing approximately 50 distinct ecosystems and numerous indigenous territories.

Place
Ecuador
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 🔘 Governance_Bodies 🪢 Network_Weaving 🔅 Traditional_Ecological_Knowledge 🌱 Vegetation_Planting 🌾 Regenerative_Agriculture 🏕️ Territorial_Monitoring 📣 Political_Advocacy 📉 Ecological_Monitoring ✅ Result_Based_Mechanisms 📊 Socioeconomic_Indicators

Background


Where the Andes' glacial peaks descend to meet the Amazon basin, an experiment in intercultural governance is taking shape across 35 million hectares of one of Earth's most biodiverse regions. The bioregion encompasses more than 50 distinct ecosystems, fed by rich hydrology flowing from Andean glaciers into the Amazon. The region plays a crucial role in carbon absorption, with 60% of the bioregion composed of protected areas and Indigenous territories, creating a unique governance landscape where conservation and indigenous sovereignty intersect.

Across these territories spanning the Ecuador-Peru border, more than 30 indigenous peoples and nationalities maintain their own territories and languages: Andas, Achuaras, Kofanes, Secoyas, Shuar, Kukama, Iquito, Siona, Kichwa, and others. While each community faces distinct challenges, they share systemic pressures from extractive industries, infrastructure development, and environmental degradation.

Origins and Network


The Amazon Sacred Headwaters Alliance was born in 2017 when indigenous nations from Ecuador and Peru issued an urgent call to protect this megadiverse bioregion. Their vision: develop a bioregional plan that articulates realistic solutions to address the economic and social challenges facing the region while protecting its ecological and cultural integrity.

The initiative maps how indigenous territories connect across national borders, creating what participants describe as a "mosaic of interculturality and plurinationality." This vision aligns with Ecuador's constitutional recognition of interculturality and plurinationality as foundational principles of the state. However, the alliance faces a fundamental challenge: Peru's legal framework differs significantly from Ecuador's, creating governance complexities when states fail to recognize indigenous rights equally.

Activities

🔸

Cross-Border Indigenous Alliance Building

The alliance is a long-horizon effort to weave together Indigenous nations on both sides of the Ecuador–Peru border—more than 30 peoples and nationalities in a region where colonial borders have often split communities and territories. The point is not a one-off summit but sustained relationship-building: recurring Indigenous-led assemblies where people bring decisions home to their own authorities; ceremonies and protocols that set the tone before policy debate; and working sessions that can host technical and political questions—land, extraction, climate—without displacing local norms with outside timetables. Over time, that rhythm of meeting has helped groups with fraught histories see themselves as a single political and cultural force. Participants describe the shift as a “marriage between peoples,” drawing on traditional approaches to conflict resolution to move from rivalry toward shared strategy.

🔸

Reforesting Edible Forests

A regenerative food forest project that increases biodiversity while providing economic benefits to 47 communities. The project supports communities while restoring forest ecosystems, creating productive landscapes that integrate food security with ecological restoration.

🔸

Amazon Headwaters Territorial Monitoring

Communities are establishing autonomous monitoring systems that combine traditional knowledge with modern technology—from satellite imagery to smartphone-based documentation—to track both ecological health and territorial incursions. This data feeds into a broader advocacy strategy aimed at influencing national and international policy, particularly around keeping fossil fuels in the ground and securing indigenous land rights.

🔸

ASHA International Advocacy

The Alliance engages in significant advocacy with national governments in the region as well as international organizations. A recent example is their campaign supporting the referendum in Ecuador to keep oil in the ground in the important Indigenous (Yasuní) region of the Amazon, which passed successfully. The Alliance is now monitoring to ensure compliance with the referendum results.

🔸

Biocultural Jaguar Credits Program

This pilot conservation program aims to create and demonstrate a fully transparent ecological-economic model that safeguards Earth's biosphere while enhancing human wellbeing. Launched in partnership with the Sharamentsa Achuar community, the program integrates indigenous stewardship with modern technology to protect jaguar habitats. Jaguars serve as an "umbrella species"—their protection indirectly protects other species in the habitat—and are classified as endangered. The program targets 10,000 hectares of critical jaguar habitat in intact Ecuadorian jungle through blockchain-verified conservation credits. A robust monitoring and reporting plan, including satellite, cameras and community monitoring, supports validation of credit issuance. The credits are based on the peer-reviewed ERA Biodiversity Stewardship Methodology and issued on the open Regen Network Registry. By the time of its launch in 2024, the program had already secured $75,000+ in pre-sale commitments, representing two-thirds of initial credit availability.

Vision and Legacy


The vision articulated toward 2030 envisions this bioregion permanently protected and restored as a living bioregion, inspired by indigenous people's stewardship vision and practices. The plan envisions people and forests flourishing with a prosperous and inclusive well-being economy. The region would contribute to reversing global warming and biodiversity loss, serving as an inspiring model for a just ecological transition.

The comprehensive approach to ecosocial transition represents a significant effort to balance environmental conservation with social development, while centering indigenous rights and knowledge systems. Its success depends on sustained political will, adequate funding, and effective implementation of the proposed mechanisms, all while maintaining the cultural and ecological integrity of the Sacred Headwaters region.

🟡 Alvelal

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

A collaborative alliance operating across over 1 million hectares in southeastern Spain, using Commonland's Four Returns Framework to reverse desertification and restore prosperity. Since 2014, AlVelAl Association has grown to more than 490 members including 280 farmers, developing regenerative businesses and coordinating landscape-scale restoration through the Altiplano Regeneration Manifesto, community machinery banks, and regenerative education programs that merge art, biodiversity, and emotional connection to land.

Bioregional Context

The Altiplano Estepario spans five districts at the intersection of Almería, Murcia and Granada, three provinces belonging to Spain's southernmost region, Andalucía. It is a semi-arid steppe and transition zone between desert and Mediterranean forest. The bioregion encompasses over 1 million hectares across more than 80 municipalities. Water has always been scarce in this landscape, yet the area has been home to human settlements for centuries. Desertification and extreme climate conditions, combined with unsustainable land management practices, have reduced local biodiversity and climate resilience, making this a challenging landscape for local communities.

Place
15506 County Road 22, Doniphan, NE 68832, United States
Network Affiliation
🟣 Commonland
Tags
📐 Participatory_Planning_and_Strategies 4️⃣ 4_Returns 🏵️ Habitat_Connectivity 🌱 Vegetation_Planting 💧 Watershed_Repair 📉 Ecological_Monitoring 🌾 Regenerative_Agriculture 👩‍🌾 Farmer_Support 🏞️ Demonstrator_Site 🛠️ Resource_Hub 💬 Peer_Learning ⛓️ Value_Chain_Development 📷 Visitor_Experiences 🎒 Learning_Programs 🎨 Art_and_Storytelling ✅ Result_Based_Mechanisms 📋 Finance_Assesments 💲 Structuring_and_Capitalization

Background

The Altiplano Estepario spans five districts at the intersection of Almería, Murcia and Granada, three provinces belonging to Spain's southernmost region, Andalucía. This landscape is a semi-arid steppe—a large area of flat unforested grassland—that forms a transition zone between desert and Mediterranean forest. The bioregion encompasses over 1 million hectares across more than 80 municipalities, creating a vast territory where water scarcity has shaped human settlement patterns for centuries.

Despite these challenging conditions, the economy today is mainly based on agriculture, with traditional farming and pastoral activities playing important cultural and economic roles. Yet the landscape tells a story of both loss and potential. Mediterranean forests once covered vast areas of the territory—trees like oaks and evergreen shrubs such as thyme and rosemary. However, desertification and extreme climate conditions, combined with unsustainable land management practices, have reduced local biodiversity and climate resilience. This leads to both social and economic losses as young people leave and entrepreneurship becomes increasingly difficult.

Origins and Network

Since 2014, Commonland's landscape partner AlVelAl has been using the 4 Returns Framework to bring together local farmers, conservationists, government, and entrepreneurs to create a common vision for the territory. The alliance is made up of several entities that have a common vision of achieving the regeneration of this territory.

![[Plan-AlVelAl-2024-5 (arrastrado).jpg]]

As one director reflects: "At the moment people move away from the region to find work. I'm inspired by being part of a project that transforms a territory for the younger generation, so that my daughters can choose to live here."

Activities

🔸

Altiplano Regeneration Manifesto

The common challenges facing the territory—environmental degradation, social loss, and economic uncertainty—inspired entities from across the region to unite and create a common manifesto. The manifesto serves dual purposes: acting within the territory to regenerate and revitalize it for maximum positive impact, and serving as a powerful tool to influence regional, national, and European policies. They have united, represented in the town councils, more than 200,000 people, creating a significant collective voice for bioregional regeneration. This manifesto is designed to inspire people from different organizations to join, while also devising ways to cooperate, create networks, and build synergy between territories to inspire each other.

🔸

Natural Ecosystems Restoration

Restoration focuses on natural areas and how they connect to working farmland. On priority sites such as La Muela, partners work to recover vegetation, soils, and water retention. On farms, agreements identify where to restore natural zones alongside production, with measures to hold water and soil and to build biodiversity. Corridor initiatives extend habitat connectivity so natural patches and productive land form a coherent mosaic.

🔸

Regenerative Agriculture Transition

One of the initial goals has been to help align stakeholders and shift from the development of almond monocultures and intensive agricultural and livestock farming practices to mainstreaming regenerative practices and developing the regional market for them. More than 100,000 hectares of rain-fed almonds grow in the AlVelAl Territory, creating huge potential for business-driven restoration. Regenerative techniques are known and work, but cultural adoption is a long-term process requiring patient support and demonstration of both ecological and economic benefits. The alliance backs the transition with education and training, farm-level assessments for farms that want to change practices, research and monitoring to document what works, demonstration farms that show regenerative management in real conditions, and early-transition support so farmers can absorb risk in the first years of change.

🔸

Ecoregenerative Certification

Ecoregenerative Certification is a voluntary standard for farms that are already organic and want to show they go further: they manage land in ways that improve soil, water, and biodiversity, not only meet organic rules. That gives farmers, cooperatives, and buyers a clearer story in the market—consumers can trust the claim because it is checked against regenerative practice, not just the word on a pack. The standard applies to the main crops of the Altiplano: tree crops such as almond, olive, pistachio, grape, and walnut; field crops such as cereals and legumes; and aromatic herbs. Rules are tuned to each farm and crop rather than applied as a one-size-fits-all list, so the same seal can mean something serious whether the holder is a grower, a cooperative, or a brand further down the chain.

🔸

Regenerative Agriculture Machinery Bank

To practice regenerative agriculture, specific machinery is needed, and not all farmers can afford the full range of machines required. Farmers in the area decided to create a community machinery bank, sharing equipment among members. The bank now counts 61 members, demonstrating how resource sharing enables broader adoption of regenerative practices. The cooperative combines equipment access with collaborative learning. They have developed a network for shared farming tips ("truquillos")—those little secrets that farmers share with each other when they have trust and complicity. This approach recognizes that knowledge sharing is as important as resource sharing in building a regenerative agricultural movement.

🔸

Regenerative Value Chain Development

The work has developed three regenerative businesses now in operation: an almond-focused company (Almendrehesa), an olive oil cooperative (Habitat), and a food platform (AlVelAl Foods) to sell regenerative products from across the territory. These businesses provide farmers with premium prices for regenerative products while supporting the transition to regenerative practices. 43 locally run businesses have benefited from increased access to new markets and value chain infrastructure, creating economic opportunities that align with ecological restoration goals.

🔸

Ecotourism Development

Tourism is developed as a way to connect visitors to landscape regeneration and local culture—not as undifferentiated growth. Programs highlight stewardship, identity, and creative engagement with the Altiplano, so that travel reinforces the same regeneration story the alliance pursues in agriculture and nature.

🔸

Education Alliance

They hold that regenerating the landscape requires a shift in how people feel and think about land. The alliance pools energy, talents, knowledge, and experience toward that end, with the vision that regeneration becomes lived practice, not only a technical agenda. They pursue two main lines of work: a shared framework of knowledge and competencies for what regenerative education means in the territory, and a social strand that stresses cohesion and cooperation—because landscapes are shared, not individual. The “Regenerando Mariposa” / “Regenerating Butterfly” concept— involving the collective planting of butterfly shaped landart sculptures made from aromatic herbs–—ties art, creativity, and biodiversity regeneration into learning that can inspire wider society.

🔸

Landscape Finance Strategy

The landscape partnership first ran a 4 Returns finance assessment with AlVelAl, allied foundations and enterprises, and Commonland—mapping real interventions and their costs. The results (to early 2025) put total identified need around €177.5 million on a five-year view, with about half of that in grant-like capital. Building on that diagnosis, AlVelAl and Commonland are developing a landscape finance strategy with partners inside the territory and beyond, testing promising mechanisms such as collaboration with the European Investment Bank, cajas rurales (rural savings banks), and other instruments still taking shape—so public, community, and private capital can meet the landscape.

Vision and Legacy

The vision by 2034 is clear: the AlVelAl Territory becomes a regenerative landscape where nature and agriculture are in balance. An ecological corridor connects the region's mountain ranges. Farms with both natural and productive lands form a mosaic of biodiversity hotspots, which act as stepping zones between natural areas. Rural abandonment is reversed as young people return and find new opportunities. The area continues to regenerate, led by a group of diverse, inspired local stakeholders.

Current progress includes: 71 initiatives including art projects, demo pilots, and farms, available to raise awareness for local communities; 216 farmers implementing improved management practices in line with regenerative agriculture; 14,509 hectares under direct improved management and restoration in combined and natural zones; and 43 locally run businesses benefiting from increased access to new markets and value chain infrastructure.

The Altiplano Estepario continues to serve as a lighthouse example of holistic landscape restoration based on the 4 Returns Framework in drylands areas, inspiring other initiatives across Spain and Portugal as they work toward creating a 4 Returns Network across the Iberian Peninsula. This approach recognizes that ecological restoration must work alongside economic activities, creating a mosaic where natural areas connect through productive landscapes managed regeneratively.

🟡 Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

A partnership of 25 organizations committed to collaborative action for Scotland's temperate rainforest. Formed to address one of the world's most biodiversity-depleted countries, the Alliance works to restore and double the size of Scotland's rainforest by 2045, creating a more resilient and better functioning ecosystem.

Bioregional Context

Scotland's temperate rainforest zone stretches along the country's western coast and islands, characterized by high rainfall, mild temperatures, and remarkable biodiversity. This globally rare ecosystem—found on only about 1% of the planet's land surface—contains ancient woodlands some more than 8,000 years old, with exceptional moss, liverwort, and lichen communities found in few other places worldwide. An estimated 30,000 hectares of rainforest remain in Scotland—a mere 2% of woodland cover and only a fraction of the area that could support rainforest.

Place
Edinburgh, Scotland, United Kingdom
Tags
🌱 Vegetation_Planting 🐉 Species_Control 🏵️ Habitat_Connectivity 🔘 Governance_Bodies ♾️ Commons_Governance_Protocols 📚 Training_and_Employment_Pathways ✅ Result_Based_Mechanisms

Background

Scotland's temperate rainforest woodlands are one of its most precious resources, some more than 8,000 years old, and all of them bursting with life. Hundreds of different species are found here in exceptional quantities, many rare elsewhere—from resident jays and woodpeckers to migrant pied flycatchers and wood warblers, from rare pearl-bordered fritillaries to badgers, red squirrels and pine martens hiding among the trees and crags. It is an incredibly rare habitat, found on only about 1% of our planet's land surface, and the west of Scotland is one of those special places with just the right conditions.

Much of Scotland's temperate rainforest has been lost over the centuries, with an estimated 30,000 hectares remaining—a mere 2% of woodland cover. Despite a plethora of environmental organisations working for decades, with thousands of members, hundreds of nature reserves and countless initiatives, Scotland is still one of the most biodiversity-depleted countries on Earth.

That loss runs deeper than the landscape—it has faded from our collective imagination too. When a community engagement officer asked a group of 27 primary-age children if they knew of the Amazon rainforest, most put their hands up. But when asked if they knew about Scotland's rainforest, only two hands went up.

Origins and Network

The Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest (ASR) was formed in 2021 to address this challenge. The Alliance now has 25 diverse partner organisations and works collaboratively with 20 more, all of whom are committed to pooling their resources for the benefit of Scotland's rainforest. Partners include a range of conservation and environmental organisations, specialist societies and government agencies. In 2021, the Scottish Government made a commitment to expand and restore Scotland's rainforest, and then worked closely with ASR to develop a strategic approach to deliver on that commitment, published in 2024.

Much of the work is about coordinating landscape-scale projects, securing long-term funding, building capacity to deliver on-the-ground work, and communicating about the rainforest and the threats it faces. The partners work together with local people to provide the expertise, resource and capacity needed to deliver the vision for Scotland's rainforest.

Activities

🔸

Landscape-Scale Restoration Projects

The Alliance has adopted 11 community-focused projects that cover more than 15% of Scotland's rainforest zone, with more coming soon. These projects include Beò Airceig (an ambitious 30,000-ha collaboration between the community and landowners in the glens surrounding Loch Arkaig), Appin Rainforest Regeneration (created by the local community development trust to deliver economic, social and environmental benefits), and Loch Lomond Rainforest Project(aiming to deliver both habitat restoration and an education programme for locals and visitors). The projects are helping to tackle some of the big issues, such as deer management, invasive non-native species, job creation and even cultural regeneration through folk festivals!

🔸

The Common Ground Forum

When the Association of Deer Management Groups first approached the Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest a few years ago, they saw potential for collaboration—something they called "the common ground." But decades of conflict between environmental groups and deer management interests had created a deep-seated lack of trust that made even conversation feel like a distant dream. They brought in the Centre for Good Relations, specialists in civic mediation. Through careful facilitation, people from all sides of upland deer management—environmental charities, government agencies, gamekeepers, private estate managers—began meeting and building relationships of trust. As the mediation process was ending, the people involved insisted they wanted to keep going, to continue the work they'd started together. In Autumn 2023, the Common Ground Forum was born. Today, the Forum has brought together more than 500 people across Scotland's upland deer management sector. They work together through respectful, constructive conversations to make better, more informed decisions about upland deer management. Last November, their work was recognized with the Innovation Award at the Nature of Scotland Awards—the first time such a diverse group of people had received this kind of recognition together. NatureScot has also recruited two new deer management roles in the rainforest.

🔸

Our Rainforest Futures

The challenge of restoring Scotland's rainforest is also about building the local capacity to do the work. Our Rainforest Futures, supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, creates jobs and skills training opportunities across the west of Scotland, ensuring that local communities have the knowledge and resources to deliver long-term habitat restoration. The project brings people together to share knowledge and learn from each other, building the skills needed for rainforest management—from invasive species control to habitat monitoring—while contributing to rural economies and community wealth.

🔸

Nature Finance for Scotland's Rainforest

The Alliance estimates that £500 million in long-term investment is needed to truly restore and expand Scotland's rainforest. To date, the Scottish Government has contributed £3.8 million towards ASR's projects, with an additional £6.3 million provided to Forestry and Land Scotland to develop a Rainforest Team and put more than 2,000 hectares of rainforest habitat on the road to recovery. While £8 million has been secured for current projects, this falls far short of what's needed. That's why ASR members are developing an innovative fundraising model that blends private and public capital. This financing mechanism creates accessible, scalable investment models to harness private capital. The project establishes a comprehensive framework including business cases for ecosystem service investments (initially focusing oncarbon credits), governance structures for scaling investment, ecological and social standards, investor integrity requirements, and community benefit protocols. The model includes: - ASR Integrity Charter: An ethical framework ensuring that financial institutions, businesses, and organizations seeking to invest in or purchase ecosystem services from rainforest restoration projects align with ASR's environmental and ethical values. The charter establishes five key requirements including verifiable net zero commitments, ethical direct activities and investments, responsible lobbying practices, human rights compliance, and fair employment standards. - ASR Project Standards Framework: A comprehensive quality assurance framework establishing verification standards for rainforest restoration projects seeking private investment through ASR's funding mechanism. The standards serve as a qualification benchmark for high-integrity natural capital projects, ensuring they deliver measurable outcomes for climate, nature, and local communities. This creates transparency for investors while maintaining ecological integrity and community benefits.

Vision and Legacy

By 2045, the vision is clear: all of Scotland's rainforest restored, its size doubled, creating a more resilient ecosystem. Local communities will be championing the rainforest, wildlife will be more diverse, and at least 30 landscape-scale projects will be working to fully restore Scotland's rainforest. A £500 million Rainforest Restoration Fund will be established, with every £1 spent on rainforest restoration bringing £2 into the local economy.

Restoring Scotland's rainforest will take decades, and the vision of a healthy network of woodlands across west Scotland is the work of generations. Yet, with so many people and organisations now working together, that possibility feels closer than ever. As one land manager put it: "I've been filled with hope by the number of different people coming together with the aim of saving the rainforest. Our rainforest really could be saved if we continue the momentum!"

🟡 Aliança Mar i Terra di Mallorca

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Bioregional regeneration work on Mallorca operates through multiple interconnected initiatives, from the quiet facilitation work of Daniel Christian Wahl to the formal Aliança Mar i Terra di Mallorca formed in 2022. The work centers on cultivating conditions for deep, place-based transformation through convening, listening, and connecting.

Bioregional Context

Mallorca is an island within the Mediterranean's Balearic archipelago. Its island nature creates what seemed like clear bioregional boundaries at first, though the work has revealed complexities in managing it as a "fractal bioregion" of various islands within an archipelago biome. The region's ecological balance and social cohesion are severely threatened by over-tourism and climate change.

Place
Palma, Balearic Islands, Spain
Network Affiliation
🟣 Commonland
Tags
🪢 Network_Weaving 📷 Visitor_Experiences 🎨 Art_and_Storytelling 🛐 Cultural_and_Spiritual_Practices 🏔️ Geographic_and_Ecological_Mapping 🚚 Regional_Sourcing 🌀 Systems_and_Resource_Mapping 🎒 Learning_Programs

Background


Mallorca's ecological balance and social cohesion are severely threatened by over-tourism and climate change. Climate change happens at a rate 20% higher in the Mediterranean than elsewhere in the world. Many of Mallorca's native species are facing existential challenges from ecological changes, such as warming seas. The boom in land speculation from tourism has also caused a rapid increase in land and housing prices, negatively affecting local communities. There is growing recognition of the need to regenerate the island's land- and seascapes and tackle negative socio-economic trends resulting from human activities.

Origins and Network


The Aliança Mar i Terra di Mallorca was formed in 2022 by a consortium of local organisations facing similar challenges who decided to work towards aligned objectives together. The alliance aims to support the regeneration of regional land and sea habitats on the island of Mallorca in the Mediterranean Sea. Support from Commonland as of 2022 enabled the alliance to start working together formally.

The alliance looks toward a more balanced socioeconomic future: a more connected community co-creating biodiverse, thriving local ecosystems; a local economy grounded in a healthy agroecosystem able to supply a substantial share of food and other resources; and a systemic view in which land and sea are addressed together.

Activities

🔸

Tourism Industry Transformation Initiative

Mallorca's economy is dominated by tourism, which comprises approximately 80% of economic activity. This creates a unique context for regeneration work—tourism is both part of the problem and a necessary intervention point. The alliance has started to work on crafting partnerships within the tourism industry in order to start catalyzing change. The work included producing documentary series highlighting regenerative practices around the island called "Isla Viva".

🔸

Sacred Pathways Revitalization Project

The project uses ancient infrastructure as a tool for contemporary environmental awareness and cultural reconnection, honoring both pre-Christian and Catholic heritage. Building on the foundation of Jaime Ferrer's "Terra, Alma, Societat" work, they co-initiated a project that brought back to life seven ancient pilgrimage routes to the holy forest of Lluc. Reviving those routes—which reach back toward pre-Christian pilgrimage and sites used by prehistoric communities up to 5,000 years ago—opened a conversation about how people engage with the landscape today.

🔸

Foodshed and Energyshed Mapping

On Mallorca, the alliance has used foodshed and energyshed mapping to trace how food and energy move through landscapes and settlements—mapping relational “footprints” rather than only administrative boundaries. The aim is practical: to surface leverage points for regenerative projects rooted in how the island actually feeds and powers itself.

🔸

Educational Work with Schools

The work is less a single education program than a series of intentional conversations across communities. Projects with schools brought Balearic teachers into a “soil, soul, and society” dialogue; parallel conversations on local food helped give rise to Slow Food Balear. Multiple intervention points have seeded connections that ripple through the island’s social and ecological systems.

Vision and Legacy


On Mallorca, this understanding informs a patient, relationship-based approach to bioregional regeneration—one that dances with the system rather than trying to control it, and that celebrates when others take up the work as their own. The work recognizes that the education and stewardship efforts of the organizations are already very strong and can be linked to physical places with active ongoing projects.

Opportunities ahead include: restoring land and seascapes holistically as interconnected systems; ending industry silos that currently reduce impact; creating a clear, long-term landscape vision that enables Mallorca to shift and diversify its economic model to the benefit of local communities and nature alike; developing new regenerative business models that bring revenues to local communities, including new eco-tourism models that involve outsiders in supporting landscape restoration; and creating greater impact through the Alliance—collaboration allows for synergies between different organisational projects and greater resilience to collective obstacles.

🟡 Acción Serrana

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website → View full page

Acción Serrana focuses on biocultural restoration, reforestation, community organizing, and building long-term ecological and cultural resilience in mountainous regions as part of the larger Acción Andina coalition.

Bioregional Context

The Sierras Grandes of Córdoba are part of the Andes' southernmost reaches, a vital source of freshwater and biodiversity. This region is threatened by deforestation, desertification, and climate change, strongly impacting indigenous and gaucho communities who rely on its ecological health.

Place
Cordoba, Argentina
Network Affiliation
🟣 BioFi Project
Tags
🌰 Seeds_and_Nurseries 🌱 Vegetation_Planting 📉 Ecological_Monitoring 📚 Training_and_Employment_Pathways 🔘 Governance_Bodies 🔀 Grants_Programs ⛓️ Value_Chain_Development

Background


In the heart of Argentina, the Sierras Grandes of Córdoba represent the southernmost extension of the Andean mountain system. This high-altitude landscape shelters the Polylepis australis forest—known locally as "tabaquillo"—the highest-growing native trees in the region, forming the highest forest on Earth. These forests are critically important: they protect watershed headwaters, improve soil quality through fallen leaves and root systems, retain soil against erosion, and provide habitat for many endemic species adapted to the harsh mountain environment.

Yet these forests face severe threats: overgrazing by cattle and other animals, forest fires, and accelerating soil erosion. For generations, this ecosystem has provided water for the province of Córdoba and supported indigenous and gaucho communities who rely on its ecological integrity. The Sierras Grandes encompass 155,000 hectares of provincial water reserve and 37,000 hectares of national park—the Quebrada del Condorito National Park and the Pampa de Achala provincial water reserve—a territory where restoration work must balance ecological recovery with cultural continuity.

Origins and Network


Acción Serrana operates as a fractal of the larger Acción Andina alliance, a large-scale multinational initiative to restore high-altitude Polylepis ecosystems across the Andean region. Founded in 2018, Acción Andina aims to restore 1 million hectares) over the next 25 years. This network operates across six countries: Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, and Argentina. Together, the alliance has planted more than 12.5 million trees, representing a coordinated effort to restore ecosystems that are critical water sources for major South American rivers.

Activities

🔸

Participatory Forest Restoration

Acción Serrana has developed a sophisticated restoration infrastructure which includes maintenance of protective fencing, seed collection, nursery construction and operation, seedling germination and transplantation, and strategic underplanting during the rainy season. They run more than 26 nurseries producing Polylepis trees across 12 operational areas, creating a supply chain for high-altitude reforestation. The work spans over 70 consecutive campaigns, resulting in more than 876,000 native trees planted across more than 290 hectares of degraded mountain landscapes. Each restoration campaign involves an extensive collaboration network: over 25 organizations including NGOs, government institutes, and businesses working together. The campaigns employ 65 permanent staff and mobilize more than 1,300 annual volunteers.

🔸

Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning

A robust monitoring system ensures transparency and scientific rigor across all restoration work. Acción Serrana maintains permanent ecological plots in 12 reforestation areas, with university-led citizen science programs tracking restoration progress. The system includes more than 8 years of technical reporting, monitoring tree growth and survival rates over five-year periods after planting. Current measurements show approximately 70% tree survival rates—a significant achievement in high-altitude environments with challenging growing conditions. The monitoring system tracks multiple indicators: hectares restored, tree survival and growth, employment generation, staff involvement, and landscape-scale ecological changes. This comprehensive approach enables adaptive management, replicability across sites, and accountability to local communities, funders, and the scientific community.

🔸

Culture and Employment

Beyond ecological goals, the restoration work focuses on promoting visibility of local gaucho and indigenous communities, creating green employment opportunities for youth in restoration, mountain guiding, and forest ranger positions. This dual approach addresses both ecosystem degradation and the need for sustainable livelihoods that keep young people connected to mountain communities.

🔸

Academia Biosférica

The Academia Biosférica program represents an intergenerational training initiative developed in partnership with institutions across Latin America. This academy will integrate ecosystem restoration education, mountain ecology, and regenerative culture practices, combining scientific knowledge with ancestral wisdom and youth leadership training. The program aims to generate ecological, economic, social, and cultural sustainability through the social inclusion of young people in ecological restoration and environmental education.

🔸

Governance and Values

Acción Serrana operates through a four-tiered governance model that reflects the bioregion's nested social and ecological systems: 1. At the most local level, community-led watershed councils organize activities across more than five basins, representing different communities and landscapes. 2. These councils feed into an intergenerational advisory board composed of local organizations, ensuring that wisdom from elders and innovation from youth both inform decision-making. 3. This local structure is articulated through the national Foundation of Biospheric Activities, which provides administrative and legal infrastructure. 4. Finally, international sponsors including the Triangle Foundation, Global Forest Generation, and others provide financial and technical support. The governance model embodies Acción Serrana's core values: ecological integrity, cultural resilience, youth inclusion, and reciprocity with nature. As one leader explains, these values are "very basic but really guiding the heterogeneity and diversity of our groups in the different basins."

🔸

Capital Allocation and Financial Strategy

Currently, approximately 70% of funding comes through Acción Andina's international network, with 30% from matching grants and public-private partnerships. The organization is actively transitioning toward more diversified blended finance mechanisms to reduce dependence on any single funding source. Grants flow to infrastructure development (nurseries, fencing), direct reforestation activities, youth employment programs, and capacity building. Sub-funds support microgrants for community initiatives, citizen science monitoring programs, and branding support for regenerative products. The allocation model ensures that decision-making power remains with local communities while accessing resources from international allies.

🔸

Regenerative Products & Services Portfolio

A developing line of bioregionally-rooted products including herbal tea blends from native species, guided eco-tourism experiences to restoration sites, and local food products. The products are developed through participatory design processes that integrate community knowledge, ecological criteria, and market opportunities. By creating value chains that circulate benefits within the bioregion, Acción Serrana reduces dependence on external funding while strengthening connections between local communities, ecosystems, and economic opportunities.

Vision and Legacy


By 2025, the organization expects to reach the milestone of 1 million trees planted in the Sierras Grandes. But the deeper impact extends beyond tree counts: the initiative has restored forests where all the water for the province of Córdoba originates, while simultaneously contributing to Acción Andina's work restoring ecosystems that feed major South American rivers. The project aims to offer a replicable approach to high-altitude forest restoration that can inform work across Andean landscapes and beyond.
